The graph has infinitely many asymptotes, and there is an infinite number of points where the function takes values of $1$ and $-1.$ We can write down general expressions for these properties, by assuming $n$ represents an integer.

**The Asymptotes of the Function**

The function has asymptotes when $x=\pm \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pm \dfrac{3\pi}{2},\ldots,$ etc. Therefore, a general equation for the asymptotes of the graph is

$$
x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi.
$$

**The Points Where the Function Takes a Value of $\mathbf{1}$**

From the graph, we see that the function takes a value of $1$ when $x=0.$ Since the function has a period of $2\pi,$ a general expression for the values of $x$ for which $\sec x = 1$ is

$$
x = 2n\pi.
$$

**The Points Where the Function Takes a Value of $\mathbf{-1}$**

Similarly, from the graph, we see that the function takes a value of $-1$ when $x=\pi.$ Since the function has a period $2\pi,$ a general expression for the values of $x$ for which $\sec x = -1$ is

$$
x = \pi +2n\pi.
$$

occurrences.title: The Periodicity Property of the Secant Function
occurrences.content:
Let's recall the graph of the function $y=\sec x\mathbin{:}$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/1aaf29d1753b7d611b12504f73362dc2)

As we've stated before, the secant function inherits its periodicity from the cosine function, so the period is $2\pi.$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/d455205729cba0e9ec79b6594a3c6c5a)

The periodicity of $y=\sec x$ means that

$$
\sec (x+2n\pi ) = \sec x
$$

for any integer $n.$

occurrences.title: Finding the Point on a Line Closest to Another Point
occurrences.content:
Consider the line $l$ with the equation $y=-x + 6$ and the point $Q(2,1)$ that does not lie on $l.$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/bba8713d2e6f6daf1d9a065fa05259f9)

Suppose we wish to find the point $P$ that lies on $l$ that's closest to the point $(2,1).$ 

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/c622859da659ebb0a729409a40e3c4d3)

Now, here's the key idea: $P$ is the point that lies on $l$ *and* lies on the line *perpendicular* to $l$ that passes through $Q.$

So, to find $P,$ we proceed as follows:

- First, we find the line perpendicular to $l$ that passes through $Q.$

- Then, we find the intersection of the two lines.

We know that one endpoint of the segment is [math](2,1).[/math] To find the other endpoint, we find the equation of the line that is perpendicular to [math]y=-x+6[/math] and passes through the point [math](2,1),[/math] and then find where it intersects [math]y=-x+6.[/math]

The line $y=-x + 6$ has a slope of $-1,$ so our perpendicular line must have a slope of $1$ (the negative reciprocal). It also must pass through the point $(2,1).$ So, using point-slope form, we find that the equation of the perpendicular line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =1\cdot (x-2) \\ y-1 & =x-2 \\ y & =x-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find where the lines $y=-x+6$ and $y=x-1$ intersect, we set the equations equal to each other and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-x+6 & =x-1 \\ 6+1 & =x+x \\ 7 & =2x \\ x & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=\dfrac{7}{2}$ into either of the two equations gives $y=\dfrac{5}{2}.$ So, the coordinates of $P$ are $\left( \dfrac{7}{2}, \dfrac{5}{2} \right).$

occurrences.title: The Shortest Distance Between a Point and a Line
occurrences.content:
Earlier, we found that the point $P\left(\dfrac72,\dfrac52\right)$ lies on the line $y=-x+6$ and is the closest point on this line to the point $Q(2,1).$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/e84fc16704b47bddb5eca3de0e21cc8d)

To calculate the shortest *distance* between $Q$ and the line, we compute the distance between $P$ and $Q$ using the distance formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{{({x}_{2}-{x}_{1})}^{2}+{({y}_{2}-{y}_{1})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{7}{2}-2)}^{2}+{(\frac{5}{2}-1)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}+\frac{9}{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the shortest distance between the line $y=-x+6$ and $Q(2,1)$ is $\dfrac{ 3 }{ \sqrt{2} } .$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
The shortest distance between a point and a line is the length of the line segment that connects the point to the line and is perpendicular to the line.

For example, consider the point ![](/tmp/newer-review/graphics/e2002597cf3d8b01e24e7b4d2c6daf6fc9afb0afb3c6140877abfc3bf1be02c4.svg) and the horizontal line ![](/tmp/newer-review/graphics/06444505f504ecd01a91d4846b46bf202caafa9d9f756958483262f69b5db14b.svg) shown below:

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/00e6be4ceac22f8d2b40f18cb429e9e9)

To find the distance between the point and the line, we construct a segment with its endpoints on the point and the line, and which is perpendicular to the line

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/22bf1ddeb287e6164959e17ff70e5355)

The distance between the point and the line is the length of this segment, which we compute as the absolute value of the difference in ![](/tmp/newer-review/graphics/1d9b846cface9f9348e4081a0dd87dd254bf26663c12aa0d1a15aa24d2393261.svg)-coordinates of the point and the line:

![](/tmp/newer-review/graphics/11e3682c2b811da299d9c475bd0ba3684d0c7f68e5677d925744b37026c47b0c.svg)

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
The equation of the normal line to the curve $y = f(x)$ at the point $P(x_1,y_1),$ in point-slope form, is given by

$$
y - y_1 = m (x - x_1), \hspace{1cm} m=-\dfrac{1}{f'(x_1)}.
$$

Here, $m=-\dfrac{1}{f'(x_1)}$ because the slope of the normal line is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line, and $f'(x_1)$ represents the slope of the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at the point $(x_1,y_1).$

For example, suppose we want to compute the equation of the normal line to the curve $y=x^2$ at the point $A(1,1).$ This normal line is the dashed line shown below, which is perpendicular to the solid tangent line. 

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/424a5b155291a888240f9e553dc0c7be)

Since $y=x^2,$ we have $f(x)=x^2.$ We begin by calculating the derivative of $f(x)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f'(x) 		 = \dfrac {\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(x^2)= 2x
$$

At $A(1,1),$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
f'(1) 	= 2(1) = 2.
$$

However, we want the normal line, and the slope of the normal line is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
m = -\dfrac{1}{f'(1)} = -\dfrac{1}{2}
$$

 

Finally, we work out the equation of the normal line using the point-slope form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =-\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+1 \\ y & =-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the normal line is $y=-\dfrac x 2 + \dfrac 3 2.$ We could also write this in standard form as $x+2y=3.$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Consider the graph of the function $y = f(x)$ shown below. 

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/a79d541e880f48f10719a568b02836d4)

Let's use our knowledge of derivatives to find $f'(0),$ the derivative of $f$ at $x=0.$

Note the following:

- $f'(0)$ represents the slope of the tangent to $y=f(x)$ at the point $x=0.$

- The function $y = f(x)$ is made up of line segments.

- So, to find $f'(0),$ we simply need to find the slope of $y = f(x)$ over an interval that contains $x=0,$ and where $f$ is represented by a single line segment.

With that in mind, we consider the graph of $y=f(x)$ over $x\in [-2,1].$ 

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/c0580267ce2c244f407adc0127ce17d9)

This interval contains $x=0,$ and $f$ is represented by a single line segment over this interval.

The slope of $y=f(x)$ over this interval is equal to

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{Δf}{Δx} & =\frac{2-1}{1-(-2)}=\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f'(0)=\dfrac{1}{3}.$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Suppose a company manager compiles the tables below, showing the years of work experience and corresponding monthly salary, in thousands of dollars, among a particular group of employees.

| **Work Experience (years)** | **$2$** | **$4$** | **$5$** | **$7$** | **$9$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Salary (thousands of $\[math]$)** | $2.5$ | $3$ | $4$ | $4.5$ | $4.5$ |

To visualize this kind of data, we can use **scatter plots**.  Let's draw a scatter plot representing the information in our table.

The first step is to set up the axes in the coordinate plane. We draw

- the *independent variable* (years of work experience) along the horizontal axis, and

- the *dependent variable* (salary) along the vertical axis.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/ec18bdc52fa826c969d6103b9a985d79)

Then, we plot the points that correspond to the pairs from the data:

$$
(2,2.5), \quad
(4,3), \quad
(5,4), \quad
(7,4.5), \quad
(9,4.5)
$$

This gives us the following scatter plot.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/ce1922c146b6697326a206627b4445d4)

occurrences.title: Axis Discontinuities
occurrences.content:
When constructing a scatter plot, choosing an appropriate scale on one (or both) coordinate axes is often impossible unless we distort or enlarge our plot considerably.

To demonstrate the issue and how to deal with it, consider the data in the following table, showing the ages and corresponding weights of five players on a baseball team.    

| **Age (years)** | **$10$** | **$11$** | **$12$** | **$13$** | **$14$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Weight (kg)** | $30$ | $40$ | $30$ | $50$ | $70$ |

Now, notice that

- the data for the independent variable (age) starts at $10$ and increases in increments of one, while

- the data for the dependent variable (weight) starts at $30$ and increases in increments of ten.

In this case, the scales for the coordinate axes of our scatter plot could be as follows: 

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/b68173b7b4063cfb713f7bb8c117be65)

The "*lightning bolt symbol*" (highlighted) at the beginning of the $x$-axis indicates a jump or **axis discontinuity**. This symbol means we omit a whole interval on the $x$-axis unrelated to the given data to set a more convenient scale.

Finally, we complete the construction of our scatter plot by plotting the points representing the data, as usual. 

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/87acd1581f8f83d2b3c556063524815b)

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Just as we can find the least common multiple ($\textrm{LCM}$) of two monomials, we can also find the least common multiple of two polynomials.

To find the least common multiple ($\textrm{LCM}$) of two polynomials that are made up of products of binomials, we find the least common multiple of the constants and the least common multiple of the variable part. Then, we multiply all of the results together.

For example, let's find the least common multiple of $6(x+3)^2$ and $8(x+3).$

First, we find the least common multiple of the constants, $\textrm{LCM}(6,8)\mathbin{:}$

- Multiples of $6 \mathbin{:}$ $\quad 6, \, 12, \, 18, \, {\color{blue}24}, \, 30, \ldots$

- Multiples of $8 \mathbin{:}$ $\quad 8, \, 16, \, {\color{blue}24}, \, 32, \ldots$

So, $\textrm{LCM}(6,8) =  {\color{blue}{24}}.$

To find the $\textrm{LCM}$ of $(x+3)^2$ and $(x+3),$ we raise $(x+3)$ to the largest power that appears in the expressions, which is $2.$ Therefore,

$$
\textrm{LCM}\left((x+3)^2, \, (x+3) \right) = {\color{red}{(x+3)^2}}.
$$

Finally, we multiply all of our results together:

$$
\textrm{LCM}\left(6(x+3)^2, \, 8(x+3) \right) = {\color{blue}{24}}\cdot {\color{red}{(x+3)^2}} = 24(x+3)^2.
$$

occurrences.title: The Periodicity Property of the Cotangent Function
occurrences.content:
Let's inspect the graph of the function $y=\cot x$ one more time.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/6b4907ee3cefda41a7b8de1d09ab72c5)

We've seen that the function $y=\cot x$ is periodic, where the period is $\pi.$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/ada757e064def0332ef6c51a33366931)

The periodicity of $y=\cot x$ means that $\cot\left( x+n\pi\right) = \cot\left( x\right)$ for any real number $x$ and for any integer $n.$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Recall the graph of the function $y=\cot x\mathbin{:}$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/18cce6796e38d6ac3f031b704fae2769)

Similarly to the tangent, the cotangent has infinitely many zeros, and the function has an infinite number of vertical asymptotes.
Let's construct general expressions for these, assuming that $n$ represents an integer.

**The Zeros of the Function**

From the graph, the function has a zero when $x=\dfrac\pi 2,$ and the function is periodic with period $\pi.$ Therefore, a general expression for the zeros is

$$
x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}+ n\pi.
$$

**The Vertical Asymptotes of the Function**

From the graph, we see that the vertical asymptotes of the function occur at $x=0,\pm\pi,\pm2\pi,\dots.$

Therefore, a general equation for the asymptotes is

$$
x = n\pi.
$$

occurrences.title: The Oddness Property of the Cotangent Function
occurrences.content:
Recall that a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if it satisfies the property

$$
f(-x) = -f(x).
$$

As it turns out, cotangent is an odd function! So, for any value of $x,$ we have

$$
\cot(-x) = -\cot(x).
$$

Odd functions always have rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin. This is indeed true of the cotangent function, as we can see from the diagram below. 

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/0321da7026052fada380eb8c03cd7229)

We can use the oddness property of cotangent in conjunction with its periodicity property to simplify trigonometric expressions. Let's see an example.

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Suppose we want to determine if the relationship between two variables is *linear*. How would we do this?
One way is to draw a scatter plot and try to find a straight line that fits the data. 

Consider the scatter plot below that shows the correspondence between the variables $x$ and $y.$ 

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/5b8c1668e17f09ce60e2420d57a4b320)

Notice that the data points are scattered along a straight line, as shown below. This line is called the **trend line**, **regression line,** or **line of best fit.** We also say that the data has a **linear trend**.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/1289f9ad719842d40b22c4261aaab6ea)

On the other hand, some data sets do *not* show a linear trend. For example, consider the following scatter plot that shows the correspondence between the variables $a$ and $b.$ 

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/c6752d42d628a90dce9a18f1765ac301)

From the plot, it seems that the data points are scattered randomly. Therefore, there is no linear trend.

occurrences.title: Justifying the Derivatives of Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions
occurrences.content:
To see why the derivative of $\sec x$ is $\sec x \tan x,$ we start by remembering that

$$
\sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}.
$$

If we now differentiate the above relation using the quotient rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sec}x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}x}) \\  & =\frac{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1)\cdot \operatorname{cos}x-1\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}x)}{{[\operatorname{cos}x]}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(0)\cdot \operatorname{cos}x-1\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}x)}{{cos}^{2}x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}x}{{cos}^{2}x} \\  & ={{\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}x}}_{⏟}}_{\operatorname{sec}x}{{\frac{\operatorname{sin}x}{\operatorname{cos}x}}_{⏟}}_{\operatorname{tan}x} \\  & =\operatorname{sec}x\operatorname{tan}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can use the same method to find the derivative of the other two reciprocal trigonometric functions,

$$
\csc x = \dfrac{1}{\sin x} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \cot x = \dfrac{1}{\tan x}.
$$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
The derivatives of the reciprocal trigonometric functions are shown in the table below:

| $f(x)$ | $f'(x)$ |
| --- | --- |
| $\sec x$ | $\sec x\tan x$ |
| $\csc x$ | $-\csc x\cot x$ |
| $\cot x$ | $-\csc^2 x$ |

As with the standard trigonometric functions, we can now differentiate any combination of the above functions using the rules of differentiation.

For example, let's find the derivative of 

$$
y= \sec x + \csc x.
$$

We can take the derivative of each term and then add them, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sec}x+\operatorname{csc}x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sec}x)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{csc}x) \\  & =\operatorname{sec}x\operatorname{tan}x-\operatorname{csc}x\operatorname{cot}x\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** We could have computed the derivative of the above function by rewriting it as

$$
y= \dfrac{1}{\cos x} + \dfrac{1}{\sin x}
$$

and applying the appropriate derivative rules. However, this would have taken significantly more work! You can save a lot of time by memorizing the derivatives of the reciprocal trigonometric functions.

occurrences.title: Mnemonic Tricks
occurrences.content:
Trigonometric functions appear very frequently in calculus, so it's extremely important to commit their derivatives to memory.

Conveniently, there are some mnemonic tricks that we can use to more easily remember the derivatives of trigonometric functions.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}x) & =\operatorname{cos}x\, & \,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}x) & =-\operatorname{sin}x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tan}x) & ={sec}^{2}x\, & \,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sec}x) & =\operatorname{sec}x\operatorname{tan}x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cot}x) & =-{csc}^{2}x\, & \,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{csc}x) & =-\operatorname{csc}x\operatorname{cot}x\end{aligned}
$$

It's helpful to notice that the "co"-functions (cosine, cosecant, and cotangent) all have negative signs in their derivatives, while the other trigonometric functions (sine, secant, and tangent) do not.

It's also helpful to realize that functions come in pairs.

- Sine and cosine are a pair because each appears in the other's derivative.

- Tangent and secant are a pair because each appears in the other's derivative.

- Cotangent and cosecant are a pair because each appears in the other's derivative.

Lastly, it's helpful to realize the following:

- Ignoring the positive or negative sign, tangent and cotangent have a similar format for their derivatives: the square of the function they're paired with.

- Ignoring the positive or negative sign, secant and cosecant have a similar format for their derivatives: the product of themself and the function they're paired with.

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
We know that the derivative of sine is cosine:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}(\sin{x}) = \cos{x}
$$

Since integration is the reverse of differentiation, we see that the integral of cosine is sine:

$$
\int \cos{x}\,\textrm d x = \sin{x} + C
$$

We can discover two other integrals by considering the derivatives of cosine and tangent:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{cos}x+C \\ \int {sec}^{2}x\text{ }\text{d}x & =\operatorname{tan}x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, by considering the derivatives of secant, cosecant, and cotangent, we arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sec}x\operatorname{tan}x\text{ }\text{d}x & =\operatorname{sec}x+C \\ \int \operatorname{csc}x\operatorname{cot}x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{csc}x+C \\ \int {csc}^{2}x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{cot}x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

With these six formulas, we can integrate many different trigonometric functions.

occurrences.title: The Oddness Property of the Cosecant Function
occurrences.content:
Recall that a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if it satisfies the property

$$
f(-x) = -f(x).
$$

As it turns out, cosecant is an odd function! So, for any value of $x,$ we have

$$
\csc(-x) = -\csc(x).
$$

Odd functions always have rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin. This is indeed true of the cosecant function, as we can see from the diagram below. 

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/6511ba7717b414bd1b6e27a0b2eab208)

We can use the oddness property of cosecant in conjunction with its periodicity property to simplify trigonometric expressions. Let's see an example.

occurrences.title: The Periodicity Property of the Cosecant Function
occurrences.content:
Let's recall the graph of the function $y=\csc x$ once more.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/3801e3b2e597fdfb3172a86cfb43ceb3)

As previously mentioned, the cosecant function inherits its periodicity from the sine function, so the period is $2\pi.$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/4048569c45b60b76858ffa94a55db24e)

The periodicity of $y=\csc x$ means that $\csc (x+2n\pi ) = \csc x$ for any number $x$ in the domain of $\csc x$ and any integer $n.$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Let's look at the graph of the cosecant function again.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/d26c20faec940b6fdeabc66a28129c0f)

The graph of the cosecant function has infinitely many asymptotes, and there is an infinite number of points where the function takes values of $-1$ and $1.$

Let's write general expressions for these properties, by assuming $n$ represents an integer.

**The Asymptotes of the Function**

The function has asymptotes when $x=0,\pm \pi, \pm 2\pi,\ldots,$ etc. Therefore, a general equation for the asymptotes of the graph is

$$
x = n\pi.
$$

**The Points Where the Function Takes a Value of $\mathbf{1}$**

From the graph, we see that the function takes a value of $1$ when $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$ Since the function has a period of $2\pi,$ a general expression for the values of $x$ for which $\csc x = 1$ is

$$
x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + 2n\pi.
$$

**The Points Where the Function Takes a Value of $\mathbf{-1}$**

From the graph, we see that the function takes a value of $-1$ when $x=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$ Since the function has a period $2\pi,$ a general expression for the values of $x$ for which $\csc x = -1$ is

$$
x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2} +2n\pi.
$$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
The chain rule can be used to differentiate trigonometric functions like 

$$
y = \sin (2x).
$$

First, notice that this function can be written as the composite function

$$
y = \sin u, \qquad u = 2x.
$$

We can use the chain rule to compute the derivative of this composite function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(\operatorname{sin}u)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}u\cdot 2 \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}u\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $u=2x,$ we obtain the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2\operatorname{cos}(2x)\end{aligned}
$$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Sometimes, we need to combine multiple rules of differentiation to differentiate a given function. As a reminder, the product rule, quotient rule, and chain rule are stated below.

- Product rule: $\hspace{.5cm} \dfrac{\mathrm{d} }{\mathrm{d}x } \left[ u(x) \cdot v(x) \right] = u'(x) \cdot v(x) + u(x) \cdot v'(x)$

- Quotient rule: $\hspace{.5cm} \dfrac{\mathrm{d} }{\mathrm{d}x } \left[ \dfrac{u(x)}{v(x)} \right] = \dfrac{u'(x)\cdot v(x) - u(x)\cdot v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2}$

- Chain rule: $\hspace{.5cm} \dfrac{\mathrm{d} }{\mathrm{d}x } \left[ u(v(x)) \right] = u'(v(x))\cdot v'(x)$

occurrences.title: The Connection Between Variance and Covariance
occurrences.content:
Variance measures the spread of a *single* data set $x$ around its mean value $\overline{x}.$ On the other hand, covariance measures the relationship between *two* data sets $x$ and $y.$

The (population) covariance of the data sets

$$
x=\big\{ x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_n \big\}, \qquad  
y=\big\{ y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n \big\}
$$

 

is given by 

$$
\textrm{Cov}(x,y) =  \dfrac{1}{n} \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})(y_i - \overline{y}).
$$

If we compare a single data set, say $x$, against itself using our formula for covariance, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}(x,x) & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}) \\  & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} \\  & ={\sigma }^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where $\sigma^2$ denotes the variance of $x.$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Given two finite data sets of equal length, say,

$$
x=\big\{ x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_n \big\}, \qquad 
y=\big\{ y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n \big\},
$$

the **covariance** between $x$ and $y,$ denoted by $\textrm{Cov}(x,y),$ is a measure that evaluates the extent to which $x$ and $y$ change together.

- A positive covariance means that if $x$ increases, then $y$ is also likely to increase:

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/a1bba23e4e22ed10cdac47ab25851c7c)

- A negative covariance means that if $x$ increases, then $y$ is likely to decrease:

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/3ab040bb792dd462b905ba4647b1dd2c)

- A covariance of zero (or close to zero) indicates that there is no *linear* relationship between $x$ and $y.$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/63b2e29927552637a81c1716b3d4b2a2)

**Watch Out!** A covariance of zero does *not* mean that $x$ and $y$ are not related. It simply means the relationship between them is not linear. To illustrate, consider the image below.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/4eb9a94c8844a472d6cc961de2dfcb48)

The (nonlinear) relationship shown above is $y=x^2.$ However, it can be shown that $\textrm{Cov}(x,y) = 0$ for this data set.

To calculate $\textrm{Cov}(x,y),$ we use the following formula: 

$$
\textrm{Cov}(x,y) =  \dfrac{1}{n} \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})(y_i - \overline{y}),
$$

where $\overline{x}$  and $\overline{y}$ denote the means of $x$ and $y$ respectively.

**Note**: This formula for the covariance assumes that $x$ and $y$ are drawn from a *population*. There is a slightly different formula for covariance when $x$ and $y$ are sample data. However, we won't worry about the difference for now.

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
The most general way of solving exponential equations with different bases is to use logarithms on both sides of the equation. 
For example, given the equation

$$
3^{x+1} = 5^{x},
$$

we could apply $\log_3$ on both sides and get

$$
\log_3(3^{x+1}) = \log_3(5^{x}).
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\log_b \left( b^c \right) = c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & ={log}_{3}({5}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law for logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x{log}_{3}(5)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x{log}_{3}(5) \\ x-x{log}_{3}(5) & =-1 \\ x(1-{log}_{3}(5)) & =-1 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{1-{log}_{3}(5)} \\ x & =\frac{1}{{log}_{3}(5)-1}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** in the first step, we also could have applied $\log_5$ on both sides of our equation, instead of $\log_3.$ Then, the answer would be numerically the same but expressed using $\log_5$ instead of $\log_3.$

### General Case

In general, let's consider an equation of the form

\[
a^{f(x)} = b^{g(x)},
\]

where [math]a[/math] and [math]b[/math] are different constants that can't be presented as powers of the same base, and [math]f(x)[/math], [math]g(x)[/math] are some functions.
We now can apply 
\[
\log_a
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\log_b
\]
as well as the common logarithm ([math]\log[/math]) or the natural logarithm ([math]\ln[/math]) on both sides of our equation to get rid of the exponents.

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Factorials can be applied to variables, too. To manipulate a factorial expression involving a variable, we just need to remember that the variable represents a number, and the previous number can be obtained by subtracting $1$ from the variable.

So, in the same way that we have

$$
\begin{aligned}5! & =5\cdot \overset{4!}{\overset{⏞}{4\cdot 3\cdot 2\cdot 1}} \\  & =5\cdot 4!\end{aligned}
$$

we also have

$$
\begin{aligned}n! & =n\cdot \overset{(n-1)!}{\overset{⏞}{(n-1)\cdot (n-2)\cdot \,⋯\,\cdot 2\cdot 1}} \\  & =n\cdot (n-1)!\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ denotes some positive integer.

Likewise, in the same way that we have

$$
5! = 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3!
$$

we also have

$$
x! = x \cdot (x-1) \cdot (x-2)!
$$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Let's recall the formula for factoring a perfect square:

$$
x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}{\color{blue}{a}}x + a^2 = (x + {\color{blue}{a}})^2
$$

As we've seen, **completing the square** on a quadratic expression means expressing it as the sum of a perfect square and a constant.

In this lesson, we'll learn how to complete the square on a quadratic expression when the coefficient of the linear term is odd. In these cases, we get a fraction in the final expression.

As an example, let's consider the following quadratic expression:

$$
\left(x^2 + 5x + \left(\dfrac 52\right)^2\right) + 1
$$

Notice that we have a perfect square in the large parentheses that we can factor as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+5x+{(\frac{5}{2})}^{2} & = \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{5}{2}x+{(\frac{5}{2})}^{2} & = \\ {(x+\frac{5}{2})}^{2} & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our original expression can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x+\frac{5}{2})}^{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's see another example.

occurrences.title: Completing the Square
occurrences.content:
Let's complete the square on the following expression: 

$$
x^2 + 3x + 4
$$

The procedure is very similar to the one we encountered when the coefficient of the linear term was even.

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with ${\color{red}{2}}$ as a factor:

$$
x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}x + {\color{purple}{4}}
$$

Now, here's the trick. We *add* and *then subtract* $\left({\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}\right)^2,$ writing the constant term ${\color{purple}{4}}$ last:

$$
x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}x  + \left({\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}\right)^2 - \left({\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}\right)^2 + {\color{purple}{4}}
$$

As a result, the first three terms now form a perfect square!

$$
\underbrace{x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}x  + \left({\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}\right)^2} - \left({\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}\right)^2 + {\color{purple}{4}}
$$

Factoring the perfect square, we get

$$
\left(x + {\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}\right)^2  - \left({\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}\right)^2 + {\color{purple}{4}}.
$$

Finally, evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+4 & = \\ {(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4}+4 & = \\ {(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4}+\frac{16}{4} & = \\ {(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+\frac{7}{4} & .\end{aligned}
$$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Let's think about how to complete the square on the following quadratic expression:

$$
- \left(x^2 + 6x+4\right)
$$

We begin by completing the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
x^2 + 6x + {\color{purple}{4}}
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with ${\color{red}{2}}$ as a factor:

$$
x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}{3}}x  + {\color{purple}{4}}
$$

Then, we add and then subtract ${\color{blue}{3}}^2,$ writing the constant term ${\color{purple}{4}}$ last:

$$
\underbrace{x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}{3}}x + {\color{blue}{3}}^2} - {\color{blue}{3}}^2 + {\color{purple}{4}}
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
(x+{\color{blue}{3}})^2 - {\color{blue}{3}}^2+ {\color{purple}{4}}
$$

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
(x+{\color{blue}{3}})^2 - 5
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}-({x}^{2}+6x+4) & =-((x+3)^{2}-5) \\  & =-(x+3)^{2}+5 \\  & =5-(x+3)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

occurrences.title: Deriving the Quadratic Formula
occurrences.content:
Consider the quadratic equation

$$
ax^2+bx+c = 0,
$$

where $a\neq 0.$ We can derive a general solution to this equation by completing the square.

First, let's subtract $c$ from both sides to isolate the variable terms:

$$
ax^2+bx = -c
$$

Since $a\neq 0,$ dividing by $a$ gives

$$
x^2 + \dfrac{b}{a}x = -\dfrac{c}{a}.
$$

Next, we complete the square on the left-hand side and move the constant terms to the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{b}{2a}x=-\frac{c}{a} \\ {(x+\frac{b}{2a})}^{2}-{(\frac{b}{2a})}^{2} & =-\frac{c}{a} \\ {(x+\frac{b}{2a})}^{2}-\frac{{b}^{2}}{4{a}^{2}} & =-\frac{c}{a} \\ {(x+\frac{b}{2a})}^{2} & =\frac{{b}^{2}}{4{a}^{2}}-\frac{c}{a}\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the terms on the right-hand side over a common factor of $4a^2,$ we get

$$
\left(x + \dfrac{b}{2a}\right)^2  = \dfrac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}.
$$

Taking the square root of both sides yields

$$
x + \dfrac{b}{2a}  = \pm \sqrt{\dfrac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}}
$$

which can be simplified as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\frac{b}{2a} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we isolate $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{b}{2a}\pm \frac{\sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}\end{aligned}
$$

which simplifies as

$$
x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}.
$$

This formula is called the **quadratic formula**. You'll learn more about how to apply the quadratic formula in future lessons.

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
We can use the method of completing the square to solve quadratic equations with leading coefficients. 

As an example, let's solve the following quadratic equation by completing the square:

$$
4x^2-8x+3 = 0
$$

First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}-8x+3 & =0 \\ 4{x}^{2}-8x & =-3 \\ 4({x}^{2}-2x) & =-3 \\ 4({x}^{2}-2\cdot 1\cdot x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}) & =-3 \\ 4[(x-1)^{2}-1] & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, expanding the brackets, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4[(x-1)^{2}-1] & =-3 \\ 4(x-1)^{2}-4 & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we isolate the perfect square by adding  $4$ to both sides and then dividing by $4\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}4(x-1)^{2}-4 & =-3 \\ 4(x-1)^{2}-4+4 & =-3+4 \\ 4(x-1)^{2} & =1 \\ (x-1)^{2} & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \sqrt{(x-1)^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}} \\ |x-1| & =\frac{1}{2} \\ x-1 & =\pm \frac{1}{2} \\ x & =1\pm \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify the solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =1-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2} \\ {x}_{2} & =1+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=\dfrac12$ and $x=\dfrac32.$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
We can apply combinations of vertical and horizontal shifts and stretches to tangent and cotangent curves.

For example, let's consider the function

$$
y = \tan(Bx) + D,
$$

where $B$ and $D$ are constants. The graph of this function is shown below.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/822cecde1286760e726aba22230f3a42)

Let's compute the values of $B$ and $D$ using our knowledge of graph transformations.

Firstly, recall that we can calculate the period $T$ of a tangent or cotangent function by considering the difference in the $x$-values between two consecutive asymptotes. Therefore, 

$$
T =  \dfrac{\pi}{6} - \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{3}.
$$

The formula for the period $T$ of the function $y = A\tan(Bx + C) + D$ is given by 

$$
T = \dfrac{\pi}{B}.
$$

By applying this formula, we can calculate the value of $B\mathbin{:}$

$$
\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\pi}{B} \quad\Longrightarrow \quad B = \dfrac{\pi}{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)} = 3
$$

The parameter $D$ represents the vertical shift of the tangent function. The graph shows that the function has been translated by $1$ unit down. Hence, $D = -1.$

Therefore, the equation of our curve is

$$
y = \tan(3x) - 1.
$$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Recall that **Euler's number,** denoted $e,$ is an irrational number whose decimal approximation is

$$
e\approx2.718\,281\,828.
$$

As we'll discover, the exponential growth curve $y=e^x$ is one of the most important curves in mathematics. Its graph is given below.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/cec84ef9213a04defabd1ee37f12b017)

Now, suppose we want to sketch the graph of $y=e^{x-3} + 1.$ 

First, we shift it $3$ units to the right to get $y=e^{x-3}.$ The $y$-intercept moves from $(0,1)$ to the point $(3,1)$ but the horizontal asymptote stays at $y=0.$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/d84b038faef6126fa2b35598925f6d38)

Then, we vertically shift it by $1$ unit up to give $e^{x-3} + 1.$ The point $(3,1)$ moves to $(3,2)$ and the horizontal asymptote moves from $y=0$ to $y=1.$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/481ea97692c89ad7c586681f09060294)

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Consider the exponential function $f(x)=2^x.$ Its domain is given by 

$$
x \in (-\infty, \infty).
$$

Because the domain consists of all real numbers, if we were to apply graph transformations to $y = f(x),$ the domain would remain unchanged.

However, applying graph transformations could affect other properties of $f(x),$ such as its range, intercepts, end-behavior, and roots. In this lesson, we will learn how to calculate the properties of transformed exponential functions.

occurrences.title: Infinite Limits of Exponential Functions
occurrences.content:
Consider the graphs of $y = 2^x$ and $y = 2^{-x}$ shown below. We will use these graphs to compute the limits at infinity.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/b74353297f24c384ed5e0930e8238b73)

Considering $y = 2^x$ first, we note that as $x \to \infty,$ the function increases without bound, and as $x \to -\infty,$ the function approaches zero. So

$$
\lim_{x\to \infty} 2^x = \infty\qquad \textrm{and}\qquad \lim_{x\to -\infty} 2^x =0.
$$

The same properties hold true for any exponential function $y=a^x$ where $a \gt 1.$

Now consider the curve $y=2^{-x}.$ We have

$$
\lim_{x\to \infty} 2^{-x} = 0\qquad \textrm{and}\qquad \lim_{x\to -\infty} 2^{-x} =\infty.
$$

Again, the same properties are true for any exponential function $y=a^{-x}$ for $a \gt 1.$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Consider the graph of $y=e^x$ below. We will use this graph to compute $\lim\limits_{x \to \, 1} e^x \, .$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/10cb3b62b88394cd36f707559e61b7d5)

From the graph, we see that as $x$ approaches $1,$ the value of $y$ approaches $e^1.$ So

$$
\lim_{x\to 1} e^x = e^1 = e.
$$

The limit of the function at a point is equal to the value of the function at that point, and this is true for *any* point, not just $x=1.$ If $c$ is any real number, we have

$$
\lim_{x\to c} e^x = e^c.
$$

In fact, *all* exponential functions have this property. For $a \gt 0$ and any real number $c,$ we have

$$
\lim_{x\to c} a^x = a^c.
$$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Suppose that we wish to solve the compound inequality 

$$
4 \le x + 2 \le 8.
$$

To solve the compound inequality, we apply the usual operations to the middle of the inequality to isolate $x.$ Keep in mind that whatever we do to the middle, we also need to do to *both* the left-hand *and* right-hand sides.

Here, we can isolate $x$ by subtracting $2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	4 & \le x + 2 \le 8 \[5pt]
	4 \,{\color{red}-}\, {\color{red}{2}} &\le x + 2 \,{\color{red}-}\, {\color{red}{2}} \le 8 \,{\color{red}-}\, {\color{red}{2}} \[5pt]
	2 &\le x \le 6
}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $2 \le x \le 6.$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Suppose we want to compute $\lim\limits_{x \to \, 1} f(x)$ for the piecewise function $f(x)$ given below.

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}\, & \text{ for }\,x<1 \\ 2\, & \text{ for }\,x=1 \\ -(x-1)^{3}+3\, & \text{ for }\,x>1\end{aligned}
$$

We begin by sketching a graph of the function:

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/ccc761bee442132a07fcdcca2dd26418)

To compute $\lim\limits_{x \to \, 1} f(x),$ we must compute the left and right-sided limits separately.

- Approaching from the left, we have $x<1,$ so we use the expression $f(x) = x^3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}{x}^{3} \\  & ={1}^{3} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Approaching from the right, we have $x>1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=-(x-1)^3+3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{+}}-(x-1)^{3}+3 \\  & =-(1-1)^{3}+3 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Because the left and right-sided limits are not equal, the overall limit does not exist: 

$$
\lim\limits_{x \to \, 1} f(x) = \text{DNE}.
$$

occurrences.title: Limits of Piecewise Functions
occurrences.content:
Suppose we want to find $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 0}f(x)$ for the piecewise function given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x)={\begin{aligned}{3}^{x+1}\, & \text{ for }\,x<0 \\ \sqrt{{x}^{2}+9}\, & \text{ for }\,x\ge 0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

To get an idea of the behavior of the function around $x=0,$ we can plot the function.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/4028b4e29449a9b6737cb607570ae5ab)

To compute $\lim\limits_{x \to \, 0} f(x),$ we must compute the left and right-sided limits separately.

- Approaching from the left, we have $x < 0,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=3^{x+1}.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}{3}^{x+1} \\  & ={3}^{0+1} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

- Approaching from the right, we have $x>0,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=\sqrt {x^2+9}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+9} \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+9} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

The left and right-sided limits both exist and are equal. So, the overall limit is

$$
\lim\limits_{x \to \, 0} f(x) =3.
$$

occurrences.title: The Range of a Transformed Sine or Cosine Function
occurrences.content:
We can determine the range of a transformed sine or cosine function by observing the effect of each transformation on the maximum and minimum values.

For example, let's determine the range of the following function:

$$
f(x)={\color{red}2}\sin\left( {\color{blue}3}x - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)+{\color{green}1}
$$

We start by writing down the range of $\sin x{:}$

$$
-1 \leq \sin x \leq 1
$$

The idea is to transform this inequality using addition, multiplication, and other operations until we arrive at the following:

$$
y_{\textrm{min}} \leq f(x) \leq y_{\textrm{max}}
$$

First, we note that *horizontal* shifts and *horizontal* stretches do not affect the range. Therefore, we can immediately state that

$$
-1 \leq \sin \left( {\color{blue}3}x - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \leq 1.
$$

Notice that the middle part is starting to look like $f(x).$ However, we must also consider the effects of the amplitude $({\color{red}2})$ and vertical shift $({\color{green}1}).$

To take care of the amplitude effects, we multiply our inequality by ${\color{red}2}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-1\le \operatorname{sin}(3x-\frac{\pi }{2})\le 1 \\ 2\cdot (-1)\le 2\cdot \operatorname{sin}(3x-\frac{\pi }{2})\le 2\cdot 1 \\ -2\le 2\operatorname{sin}(3x-\frac{\pi }{2})\le 2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to deal with the vertical shift, we increase all the quantities in our inequality by $+{\color{green}1}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-2\le 2\operatorname{sin}(3x-\frac{\pi }{2})\le 2 \\ -2+1\le 2\operatorname{sin}(3x-\frac{\pi }{2})+1\le 2+1 \\ -1\le 2\operatorname{sin}(3x-\frac{\pi }{2})+1\le 3\end{aligned}
$$

Since the middle part of the inequality is now identical to $f(x),$ we can write

$$
-1  \leq f(x)  \leq 3
$$

Therefore, the range is $f(x)\in [-1,3].$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Suppose we have a transformed *sine* function whose graph is shown below.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/26ade011955106aa87cf09a3df32de10)

A transformed sine function in its most general form can be expressed as

$$
y={\color{red}A}\sin\left( {\color{blue}B} x + C\right) +{\color{green}D},
$$

where ${\color{red}A}, {\color{blue}B}, C,$ and ${\color{green}D}$ are all constants.

We can determine its properties from this general form as follows:

- The amplitude is $\vert {\color{red}A}\vert.$

- The period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{\color{blue}B}.$

- The vertical shift is ${\color{green}{D}}.$

The phase shift (horizontal shift) is slightly trickier to work out. First, we must factor the constant $\color{blue}B$ in the argument of the function as follows:

$$
y={\color{red}A}\sin\left( {\color{blue}B}\left[ x + \dfrac {C}{ \color{blue}B}\right]\right) +{\color{green}D}
$$

From here, we can see that the phase shift (or **phase**) is $-\dfrac{C}{\color{blue}B}.$

The **midline** is the horizontal line that lies halfway between the horizontal lines $y = y_{\textrm{max}}$ and $y = y_{\textrm{min}},$ where $y_{\textrm{max}}$ and $y_{\textrm{min}}$ are the maximum and minimum values of our trigonometric function, respectively. Its equation is given by

$$
y = {\color{green}{D}}.
$$

We can also think of the midline as representing the average of the maximum and minimum values. Thus, an alternative form for the midline equation is

$$
y = \dfrac{ y_{\textrm{max}} +  y_{\textrm{min}}}{2}.
$$

Finally, we can apply the same methods to determine the properties of a transformed cosine function of the form 

$$
y={\color{red}A}\cos\left( {\color{blue}B} x + C\right) +{\color{green}D}.
$$

occurrences.title: A Worked Example
occurrences.content:
Remember that to test for continuity of $f(x)$ at a point $x=c$, we need to check three conditions:

- Does $f(c)$ exist?

- Does $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}f(x)$ exist?

- Does $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}f(x) = f(c)?$

Let's use these three conditions to show that the following function is continuous at $x=1.$

$$
{\begin{aligned}1+x, & x\le 1 \\ 3-x & x>1\end{aligned}
$$

We check all three conditions in turn.

- Using the expression for the first branch of the function, we obtain that 

$$
f(1)= 1+1= 2.
$$

So, $f(x)$ is defined at $x=1.$ $\:\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$

- By calculating the one-sided limits, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}(1+x) \\  & =1+1 \\  & =2 \\ {lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}(3-x) \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

As a result:

$$
\lim\limits_{x\to 1^-} f(x) = \lim\limits_{x\to 1^+} f(x)
$$

Therefore, the limit of $f(x)$ at $x=1$ exists: 

$$
\lim\limits_{x \to 1} f(x) = 2 \:\:{\color{green}\checkmark}
$$

- We have that $\lim\limits_{x \to 1} f(x) = 2 = f(1).$ $\:\: {\color{green}\checkmark}$

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=1.$ The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown below.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/225c7965ee8651897f2919c78dcc3e1d)

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Intuitively, a function $f(x)$ is **continuous** if we can draw $y=f(x)$ without taking our pen off the paper. 

We can give a precise mathematical definition of continuity using limits:

> *A function $f(x)$ is **continuous at the point** $\boldsymbol{x=c}$ if*
> 
> 
> $$
> \lim_{x\to c}f(x) = f(c).
> $$

In other words, a function is continuous at a point if the limit at the point is equal to the function value at the point.

To test for continuity of $f(x)$ at a point $x=c$, we need to check three conditions:

- Does $f(c)$ exist? In other words, we must check that $f(x)$ is defined at $x=c.$

- Does $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}f(x)$ exist? In other words, we have to check that $\displaystyle \lim_{x \to c^{-}}f(x) = \lim_{x \to c^{+}}f(x).$

- Does $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}f(x) = f(c)?$

If the answer to all three questions is yes, then the function is continuous at $x=c.$ If the function is not continuous at $x=c,$ we say that it has a **discontinuity** at $x=c.$

The diagram below shows a function that's continuous at $x=c.$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/b5698f3a7fca75dd6653326e3f9ea4d8)

Notice that:

- $f(c)$ exists$\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$

- $\lim\limits_{x\to c}f(x)$ exists $\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$

- $\lim\limits_{x\to c}f(x) = f(c)$ $\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$

Let's now see how to use these continuity conditions to check for continuity in a piecewise function.

occurrences.title: Make Predictions Using the Trend Line Equation
occurrences.content:
If we know the equation of a trend line, we can make more accurate predictions about a given data set. Let's consider an example.

The pediatric unit of a hospital wants to know the relationship between the age $x$ (in years) and weight $y$ (in kilograms) of their patients. They collected data over several weeks and plotted the diagram given below. 

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/f60d739939ff6830f5984724980f2a95)

The hospital finds that the trend line equation is $y = 2x+8.$

Now, suppose the hospital wants to estimate the weight of a $3$-year-old child.  To do this, we substitute $x=3$ into the equation of the trend line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2x+8 \\  & =2(3)+8 \\  & =6+8 \\  & =14.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Therefore, our model predicts that a typical $3$-year-old patient weighs approximately $14\,\textrm{kg}.$

Note the following:

- There is a point on our trend line where $x=3.$ Therefore, the result $y=14$ should be reliable since we can see from the graph that the data follows a linear trend for values of $x$ close to $3.$

- Making predictions inside the range of values from which the data was collected is known as **interpolation**.

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
We can use trend lines to predict values for data that follows a linear trend.

Consider the scatter plot below that gives the correspondence between the variables $x$ and $y.$ Let's predict the value of $y$ when $x = 5.$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/d880cf5957f5545e2c0adc8a67aa5227)

First, we sketch the trend line. If we don't know the trend line's equation, then we simply approximate it.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/792f0986d523311f552d7316db5076b1)

To make our prediction, we proceed as follows:

- First, we start at $x = 5$ on the $x$-axis.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/e045ed9d1f3c9b4b17aa8248ed7599b3)

- Then, we move up until we intersect the trend line.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/be89dbddd427d0e462d0bd73f0e9dc64)

- Finally, we move left until we intersect the $y$-axis.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/e61003da130f963bb021e17395c2c277)

Therefore, when $x = 5,$ we obtain $y \approx 10.$

occurrences.title: Extrapolation
occurrences.content:
![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/657ca8c047ca69ad390f82d47dd89ff9)

Now suppose that the hospital wants to estimate the weight of a $7$-year-old child. They have no data for this age. However, if they assume that the trend continues, they can find the corresponding weight by substituting $x=7$ into the trend line equation. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2x+8 \\  & =2(7)+8 \\  & =14+8 \\  & =22.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Therefore, our model predicts that a typical $7$-year-old child weighs approximately $22 \, \textrm{kg}.$

**Warning:** The point where $x=7$ is not shown on our trend line. Therefore, the result $y=22$ *may be unreliable* since we don't know whether values of $x$ close to $7$ follow the same linear trend. The diagram below shows some trends the data *might* follow beyond our initial data range.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/ac238908ebe0bc9b4bd5c33e4e020637)

Making predictions outside the range of values from which the data was collected is known as **extrapolation**.

We must be very cautious when extrapolating in real-world situations.

occurrences.title: Extreme Values of the Sine Function
occurrences.content:
We'll now turn our attention to the minima and maxima of transformed sine and cosine functions. 

First, recall the graph of $y=\sin{x}$ once again.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/3b88a5fd007bc58ab53b7cffd9ec709b)

Recall that:

- The function has a maximum when $x=\dfrac\pi 2$ and the function is periodic with period $2\pi.$ Therefore, a general expression for the $x$-values that maximize sine is

$$
x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + 2n\pi.
$$

- The function has a minimum when $x=-\dfrac\pi 2$ and the function is periodic with period $2\pi.$ Therefore, a general expression for the $x$-values that minimize sine is

$$
x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2} + 2n\pi.
$$

occurrences.title: Extreme Values of the Cosine Function
occurrences.content:
Now, recall the graph of $y=\cos x{:}$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/a2dcfcc5e8d56a223c24184eb5e6dd41)

- The function has a maximum when $x=0$ and is periodic with period $2\pi.$ Therefore, a general expression for the $x$-values that maximize cosine is

$$
x = 2n\pi.
$$

- The function has a minimum when $x=\pi$ and is periodic with period $2\pi.$ Therefore, a general expression for the $x$-values that minimize cosine is

$$
x = \pi + 2n\pi.
$$

Let's now apply these results to transformed sine and cosine functions.

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to construct expressions that describe the zeros, maxima, and minima of transformed sine and cosine functions.

First, let's recall the following facts:

- The zeros of the sine function $y = \sin x$ are given by 

$$
x = n\pi
$$

where $n$ is any integer.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/fe93f4bd5b9f15537606436389c67aff)

- The zeros of the cosine function $y = \cos x$ are given by 

$$
x = \dfrac\pi2 + n\pi
$$

where $n$ is any integer.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/4676ef0d3a117d4efb44478a7d2961a8)

Let's use these facts to find the zeros of a transformed sine or cosine function.

occurrences.title: A Worked Example
occurrences.content:
Let's find a general expression that describes all of the zeros of 

$$
y = 5\cos \left( 2x - \dfrac{\pi}{3} \right).
$$

 

First, let's start by defining a new variable $X$ as

$$
X = 2x - \dfrac{\pi}{3}.
$$

So, we now need to calculate the zeros of 

$$
y = 5\cos X.
$$

As we saw previously, the zeros of this function are given by the expression

$$
X = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi,
$$

where $n$ is any integer.

So, to find the zeros of our original function $y = 5\cos \left( 2x - \dfrac{\pi}{3} \right),$ we rewrite $X$ in terms of the original variable $x$ and solve the resulting equation for $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}X & =\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi  \\ 2x-\frac{\pi }{3} & =\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi  \\ 2x & =\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi +\frac{\pi }{3} \\ 2x & =\frac{5\pi }{6}+n\pi  \\ x & =\frac{5\pi }{12}+\frac{n\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the zeros of $y = 5\cos \left( 2x - \dfrac{\pi}{3} \right)$ are given by 

$$
x = \dfrac{5\pi}{12} + \dfrac{n\pi}{2}
$$

 where $n$ is any integer.

Let's look at an example involving the sine function.

occurrences.title: Using Substitution
occurrences.content:
We can also use the substitution method to solve systems of equations containing fractional coefficients.

We proceed as follows:

- First, we multiply both equations by the lowest common denominator of the fractions in the system.

- Then, we apply the substitution method as usual.

Let's see an example.

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Sometimes, we might have a system of equations with fractional coefficients, such as the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{5}{4}y=-4 \\ 7x-5y=-2\end{aligned}
$$

We can turn the system into an equivalent system involving only integer coefficients. This will make it easier to solve.

In general, we multiply each equation by its lowest common denominator. In this instance, multiplying the first equation by the lowest common denominator of the fractions $(4)$ will do the job:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{5}{4}y=-4 & |\,\times 4 \\ 7x-5y=-2 & \end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve the system using, for example, the elimination method. Notice that the $5y$ term in the first equation can cancel with the $-5y$ term in the second equation.

Adding the two equations eliminates the $y$-variable, and allows us to solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+\cancel{5y} & =-16 \\ 7x-\cancel{5y} & =-2 \\ 9x & =-18 \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $x=-2$ into the equation $7x - 5y= -2$ to solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}7x-5y & =-2 \\ 7(-2)-5y & =-2 \\ -14-5y & =-2 \\ -5y & =12 \\ y & =-\frac{12}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=-2, \,y=-\dfrac{12}{5}.$

occurrences.title: Right Continuity
occurrences.content:
A function $f(x)$ is said to be **right-continuous** at the point $x=c$ if the right-sided limit is equal to the function value:

$$
\lim\limits_{x\to c^+} f(x) = f(c).
$$

To demonstrate, let's consider the function $y=f(x)$ defined on the interval $[-2,\infty)$ as shown below.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/8cdc9773c6fc461c78e751dff5d8a510)

The function is **right-continuous** at $x=-2$ because

$$
\lim_{x\to -2^+}f(x) = 4 = f(-2).
$$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
A function $f(x)$ is said to be **left-continuous** at the point $x=c$ if the left-sided limit is equal to the function value:

$$
\lim\limits_{x\to c^-} f(x) = f(c).
$$

To demonstrate, let's consider the function $y=f(x)$ defined on the interval $(-\infty,2]$ as shown below.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/1aade105a723ee84567208527881a116)

Notice that at $x=2,$ the left limit exists, while right limit does not exist because $f(x)$ is not defined for $x>2.$

$$
\lim_{x\to 2^-}f(x) = 4, \qquad \lim_{x\to 2^+}f(x) = \text{DNE}
$$

Because the right-sided limit does not exist, the overall limit does not exist either:

$$
\lim_{x\to 2}f(x) = \text{DNE}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ is not continuous at $x=2.$ However, because the left-sided limit exists and is equal to the function value at $x=2,$ i.e.,

$$
\lim_{x\to 2^-}f(x) = 4 = f(2),
$$

we can say that the function is **left-continuous** at $x=2.$

occurrences.title: Defining Continuity in Terms of Left-Continuity and Right-Continuity
occurrences.content:
Recall that a function $f(x)$ is said to be **continuous** at a point $x=c$ if 

$$
\lim\limits_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c) .
$$

In order for the above statement to be true, we require both

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {c}^{-}}f(x)=f(c)\,\text{and}\,{lim}_{x\to {c}^{+}}f(x)=f(c).\end{aligned}
$$

The above equalities represent left-continuity and right-continuity. So, we have the following fact:

> A function is **continuous** at a point if and only if it is *both* **left-continuous** *and* **right-continuous** at that point.

occurrences.title: The Domain and Asymptotes of a Transformed Function
occurrences.content:
If we are given the equation of a transformed secant or cosecant function,

$$
y={\color{red}A}\sec\left( {\color{blue}B} x + C\right) +{\color{green}D} \quad \textrm{or} \quad y={\color{red}A}\csc\left( {\color{blue}B} x + C\right) +{\color{green}D},
$$

 we can find a general expression for some of its properties, such as the asymptotes, local maxima and minima, and the domain.

To do this, we set the argument of the function $({\color{blue}B} x + C)$ equal to an expression that represents the desired property.

Let's see this idea in action.

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Given the equation of a general transformed secant function

$$
y={\color{red}A}\sec\left( {\color{blue}B} x + C\right) +{\color{green}D},
$$

some properties of the graph of the function are as follows:

- the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{\color{blue}B}$

- the vertical shift is ${\color{green}D}$

We obtain the horizontal shift by factoring the argument of the function. 

$$
y={\color{red}A}\sec \left( {\color{blue}B}\left[ x + \dfrac{C}{{\color{blue}B}} \right]\right) +{\color{green}D}
$$

From here, we can see that the phase (horizontal shift) is $-\dfrac{C}{{\color{blue}B}}.$

We can apply the same ideas to work out the properties of a transformed cosecant function of the form

$$
y={\color{red}A}\csc\left( {\color{blue}B} x + C\right) +{\color{green}D}.
$$

occurrences.title: The Range of a Transformed Secant or Cosecant Function
occurrences.content:
Remember that the range of the secant and cosecant functions is $f(x) \in (-\infty, -1] \cup [1,\infty).$

To determine the range of a transformed secant or cosecant function, we need to check each transformation's effect on both of these intervals.

For example, to find the range of

$$
f(x)={\color{red}2}\sec\left( {\color{blue}3}x + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)+{\color{green}1},
$$

we start with the range of the secant function:

$$
\sec x \in (-\infty, -1] \cup  [1, \infty)
$$

Note that horizontal shifts and stretches have no effect on the range. Therefore,

$$
\sec\left({\color{blue}3}x + \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right) \in (-\infty, -1] \cup  [1, \infty)
$$

We can split this into two inequalities:

$$
\sec\left({\color{blue}3}x + \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right)\leq -1, \qquad \sec\left({\color{blue}3}x + \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right)\geq 1
$$

To find the range of $f(x),$ we consider both intervals separately.

- Multiplying the first inequality by ${\color{red}2}$ and adding ${\color{green}1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{sec}(3x+\frac{\pi }{2})\le -1 \\  & 2\operatorname{sec}(3x+\frac{\pi }{2})\le -2 \\  & 2\operatorname{sec}(3x+\frac{\pi }{2})+1\le -1 \\  & f(x)\le -1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Multiplying the second inequality by ${\color{red}2}$ and adding ${\color{green}1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{sec}(3x+\frac{\pi }{2})\ge 1 \\  & 2\operatorname{sec}(3x+\frac{\pi }{2})\ge 2 \\  & 2\operatorname{sec}(3x+\frac{\pi }{2})+1\ge 3 \\  & f(x)\ge 3.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining both inequalities, we get

$$
f(x) \leq -1, \qquad f(x) \geq 3.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the range is $f(x)\in (-\infty, -1] \cup [3, \infty).$

occurrences.title: Local Maxima and Minima of a Transformed Function
occurrences.content:
The secant and cosecant functions have a local minimum on each of the positive branches when the function value is equal to $1,$ as shown below:

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/d75ab58c181cdcc3f14117602b5b9c8f)

Similarly, the functions have a local maximum on each of the negative branches when the function value is equal to $-1\mathbin{:}$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/163024c35bd183b34762322bf98f3dcb)

However, the values at the local minimum and maximum points of a transformed secant or cosecant function change according to the applied transformations.

For instance, let's find the value of $f(x)={\color{red}2}\sec\left( {\color{blue}3}x + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)+{\color{green}1}$ at its local minimum points.

On a positive branch of the graph of $y=\sec x,$ we have

$$
\sec x \geq 1.
$$

The points where $\sec x = 1$ are local minima of the graph of $y=\sec x.$ 

Horizontal shifts and stretches have no effect on the range. Therefore,

$$
\sec\left({\color{blue}3}x + \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right) \geq 1.
$$

Multiplying the above inequality by ${\color{red}2}$ and adding ${\color{green}1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{sec}(3x+\frac{\pi }{2})\ge 1 \\  & 2\operatorname{sec}(3x+\frac{\pi }{2})\ge 2 \\  & 2\operatorname{sec}(3x+\frac{\pi }{2})+1\ge 2+1 \\  & f(x)\ge 3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x) = 3$ at the local minimum points.

occurrences.title: Continuity Over Semi-Open Intervals
occurrences.content:
Let's take a look at the function $y=f(x)$ below.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/77e93a3d815711359a7c0069b53d5c7a)

We say that $y=f(x)$ is **continuous over the interval** $(-2,2]$ because it is

- continuous over the interval $(-2,2),$ and

- left-continuous at $x=2.$

Similarly, let's consider the graph of $y=g(x)$  below.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/63f8c786b858906170b946d26dec3b87)

We say that $y=g(x)$ is **continuous over the interval** $[-2,2)$ because it is

- continuous over the interval $(-2,2),$ and

- right-continuous at $x=-2.$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Let's consider the function $y=f(x)$ defined on the open interval $x\in(-2,2),$ as shown below.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/67a5b5433394a57a17a3bcf4d74a77d5)

The function is continuous at every point in its domain. So, we say that the function is **continuous on the (open) interval** $(-2,2).$ 

In addition, the function is continuous on any open subinterval of $(-2,2).$ For example, the open intervals 

$$
(-2,-1),\quad (0,1),\quad (0,2),
$$

etc, are all **intervals of continuity** of $y=f(x).$

Let's compare this to the very similar function $y=g(x)$ given below.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/0cea46a4ee393e08c77fe6c5a8b56dc4)

The function $y=g(x)$ is also defined on the entire open interval $(-2,2),$ but there is a point of discontinuity at $x=0.$ The function is continuous everywhere else.

For this reason, we say that the function $g(x)$ is continuous on the intervals $(-2,0)$ and $(0,2).$

occurrences.title: Continuity on a Closed Interval
occurrences.content:
Let's now take a look at the function $y=f(x)$ defined on the closed interval $[-2,2],$ shown below.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/c52b77bef1611d539f547b46c7252492)

Notice that the function $f(x)$ is

- continuous on the open interval $(-2,2)$,

- right-continuous at the endpoint $x=-2$, and

- left-continuous at the other endpoint $x=2.$

For the above reasons, we say that the function $f(x)$ is **continuous over the (closed) interval** $[-2,2].$ It is also continuous on any (open or closed) subinterval of this interval.

In general, a function $f(x)$ is said to be continuous over the interval $[a,b]$ if it is

- continuous on the open interval $(a,b),$

- right-continuous at $x=a,$ and

- left-continuous at $x=b.$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Given the equation of a general transformed tangent function

$$
y={\color{red}A}\tan\left( {\color{blue}B} x + C\right) +{\color{green}D},
$$

some properties of the graph of the function are as follows:

- The period is $\dfrac{\pi}{\color{blue}B}.$

- The vertical shift is ${\color{green}D}.$

We obtain the horizontal shift by factoring the argument of the function, as follows:

$$
y={\color{red}A}\tan\left( {\color{blue}B}\left[ x + \dfrac{C}{{\color{blue}B}} \right]\right) +{\color{green}D}
$$

From here, we can see that the phase (horizontal shift) is $-\dfrac{C}{{\color{blue}B}}.$

We can apply the same ideas to work out the properties of a transformed cotangent function of the form

$$
y={\color{red}A}\cot\left( {\color{blue}B} x + C\right) +{\color{green}D}.
$$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Some linear equations have **infinitely many solutions.** 

For example, consider the following equation: 

$$
x+5 = x + 5
$$

Let's attempt to solve this equation by subtracting $x$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & =x+5 \\ x+5-x & =x+5-x \\ 5 & =5\end{aligned}
$$

So, what does $x$ equal? The statement $5=5$ is *always* true, irrespective of the value of $x.$ This tells us that *any* value of $x$ is a solution to the equation!

Don't believe it? If we substitute any value, say $x=3,$ into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & =x+5 \\ 3+5 & =3+5 \\ 8 & =8.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

It's important to note that substituting *any* value for $x$ into the equation will lead to a true statement. For example, the values 

$$
x=42,\qquad x=-\dfrac 1 4, \qquad x=1.2345
$$

are *all* solutions to the original equation.

To summarize:

- Our original equation has *infinitely many solutions.*

- The solution of the equation is "*any (real) value of* $x$".

occurrences.title: Problems Involving Unknown Parameters
occurrences.content:
Consider the equation

$$
2qx = 10x,
$$

where $q$ is a constant. If we're given that this equation has infinitely many solutions, how can we find the value of $q?$

Notice that this equation is in the form $ax = bx{:}$

$$
\underbrace{2q}_{\large a} \ x = \underbrace{10}_{\large b} \ x
$$

In this case, 

$$
a = 2q, \qquad b = 10.
$$

We know that an equation of the form $ax = bx$ has infinitely many solutions whenever $a=b.$ Therefore, the equation has infinitely many solutions if

$$
2q = 10.
$$

Solving this for $q,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2q & =10 \\ \frac{2q}{2} & =\frac{10}{2} \\ q & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation $2qx = 10x$ has infinitely many solutions if $q = 5.$

We can check that this answer is correct by substituting $q = 5$ into our original equation. Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2qx & =10x \\ 2(5)x & =10x \\ 10x & =10x\end{aligned}
$$

and simplifying this equation by subtracting $10x$ from both sides yields

$$
\begin{aligned}10x & =10x \\ 10x-10x & =10x-10x \\ 0 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

which is true for all values of $x.$

**Note:** The constant $q$ in this problem is sometimes called a **parameter.**

occurrences.title: Problems Involving Unknown Parameters in General Linear Equations
occurrences.content:
Consider the equation

$$
(s - 2)x + t = 6x + 9,
$$

where $s$ and $t$ are constants. Given that this equation has infinitely many solutions, how can we find the values of $s$ and $t?$

Notice that this equation is in the form $ax+b = cx+d{:}$ 

$$
\underbrace{(s-2)}_{\large a} \ x + \underbrace{t}_{\large b} = \underbrace{6}_{\large c} \ x + \underbrace{9}_{\large d}
$$

We know that an equation of the form $ax+b = cx+d$ has infinitely many solutions when $a=c$ and $b=d.$

So, to determine the values of $s$ and $t$ such that the equation

$$
({\color{blue}{{s - 2}}})x + {\color{red}{{t}}} = {\color{blue}{{6}}}x + {\color{red}{{9}}}
$$

has infinitely many solutions, we **equate the coefficients** of $x,$ and we **equate the constants:**

- Equating the coefficients of $x,$ we have

$$
{\color{blue}{{s - 2}}} = {\color{blue}{{6}}}.
$$

Solving this equation for $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

- Equating the constants, we get

$$
{\color{red}{{t}}} = {\color{red}{{9}}}.
$$

Therefore, if $s = 8$ and $t=9,$ our original equation has infinitely many solutions.

occurrences.title: Conditions for a General Linear Equation To Have Infinitely Many Solutions
occurrences.content:
Each of the following equations has infinitely many solutions:

$$
2x + 1 = 2x + 1, \qquad \dfrac13x -2 = \dfrac13x -2, \qquad 1-x = 1 - x
$$

More generally, suppose we have an equation of the form

$$
ax + b = cx + d,
$$

where $a, b, c,$ and $d$ are constants. Then, this equation has infinitely many solutions if 

$$
a = c\quad \text{and}\quad b = d.
$$

Note that if we substitute $c=a$ and $d=b$ into this equation, we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}ax+b & =cx+d \\ ax+b & =(a)x+(b) \\ ax+b & =ax+b\end{aligned}
$$

Simplifying this equation by subtracting $ax$ from both sides of the equation gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}ax+b & =ax+b \\ ax+b-ax & =ax+b-ax \\ b & =b\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation, $b = b,$ is always true. Therefore, the equation has infinitely many solutions, and any real value of $x$ is a solution.

occurrences.title: Conditions for an Equation To Have Infinitely Many Solutions
occurrences.content:
Suppose we have an equation of the form

$$
ax = bx,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. If $a = b,$ then the equation has infinitely many solutions.

For example, each of the following equations has infinitely many solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x=2x,\,\frac{1}{3}x=\frac{1}{3}x\,-2.16x=-2.16x\end{aligned}
$$

To show that the general equation $ax = bx$ has infinitely many solutions whenever $a=b,$ we can substitute $a$ for $b$ in our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}ax & =bx \\ ax & =(a)x \\ ax & =ax\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we simplify this equation by subtracting $ax$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}ax & =ax \\ ax-ax & =ax-ax \\ 0 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The equation, $0=0,$ is always true, regardless of the value of $x.$ Therefore, the equation $ax = bx$ has infinitely many solutions whenever $a=b,$ and any value of $x$ is a solution to the equation.

occurrences.title: Case of Extended Bases
occurrences.content:
We can draw exactly three heights (or altitudes) in any triangle. However, sometimes the height lies outside the triangle.

To demonstrate, consider $\triangle{ABC}$ below.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/aef0343d5ac6b664576295c5fe2b4bbc)

The height corresponding to $\overline{BC}$ is a line segment that 

- runs from the opposite vertex $A$ to the line $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{BC},$ and

- is perpendicular to $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{BC}.$

In this case, it's impossible to draw a perpendicular from $A$ to the *segment* $\overline{BC}.$ However, we can first *extend* the line segment $\overline{BC}$ as follows:

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/e46336f1f9a691186f36ee0a90d2bba0)

Now, we draw the perpendicular from $A$ to $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{BC}.$ This gives the height $\overline{AH}{:}$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/8eac55836ebbc17fd3ef5f83fa73d6bb)

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Consider $\triangle ABC$ shown below. 

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/b5af9654f5193bc37076da9ee02b98f4)

Now, let's draw a line segment that 

- runs from $\color{blue}C$ to the line ${\color{red}\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{AB}},$ and

- is *perpendicular* to ${\color{red}\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{AB}}.$

This line segment is the dashed segment shown below:

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/961ab422d519e44240a391415015b403)

Finally, let's label the other endpoint of our segment ${\color{blue}{H}}.$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/af1789a4b540ac8c3334b5c084d064a1)

Note the following:

- The line segment ${\color{blue}\overline{CH}}$ is called the **height** (or **altitude**) *corresponding to* ${\color{red}\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{AB}}.$

- The line $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{AB}$ is called the **base** of the altitude ${\color{blue}\overline{CH}}.$

As we'll soon discover, the heights and their corresponding bases are important attributes of triangles.

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
**Speed** is a special unit rate applied to moving objects. It is defined as *the distance traveled per unit of time*.

We can calculate the speed of a moving object using the following equation:

$$
\text{speed} = \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}
$$

For example, suppose that a car travels $80$ miles in $2$ hours at a constant rate. What is the speed of the car? 

To find the speed (in miles per hour), we divide the number of miles, $80,$ by the number of hours, $2.$ This gives

$$
\dfrac{80}{2} = 40.
$$

Therefore, the speed of the car is $40$ miles per hour.

occurrences.title: Calculating the Total Time an Object is in Motion
occurrences.content:
Let's recall the formula relating distance to speed and time:

$$
\text{speed} \times \text{time} = \text{distance}
$$

Using the relationship between multiplication and division, we can write this equation as

$$
\text{time} = \text{distance} \div \text{speed}
$$

which is equivalent to the formula

$$
\text{time} = \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}.
$$

We can use this formula to calculate the time taken for an object moving at a particular speed to cover a certain distance. 

For example, suppose a plane flew for $3\,120$ kilometers at a constant speed of $520$ kilometers per hour. For how long was the plane in motion?

To determine the time the plane was in motion, we divide the distance, $3\,120$ kilometers, by the speed, $520$ kilometers per hour. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{time} & =\frac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}} \\  & =\frac{3\,120}{520} \\  & =\frac{3\,120÷10}{520÷10} \\  & =\frac{312}{52} \\  & =312÷52 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the plane was in motion for $6$ hours.

occurrences.title: Calculating the Distance Traveled by an Object
occurrences.content:
Let's return to the example of a car traveling at ${\color{red}{40}}$ miles per hour. 

If the car travels at this speed, it covers  a distance of ${\color{red}{40}}$ miles *every hour*. Therefore, we can deduce the following:

- after ${\color{blue}{1}}$ hour, the car covers a distance of ${\color{red}{40}}\times{\color{blue}{1}} = 40$ miles

- after ${\color{blue}{2}}$ hours, the car covers a distance of ${\color{red}{40}}\times{\color{blue}{2}} = 80$ miles

- after ${\color{blue}{3}}$ hours, the car covers a distance of ${\color{red}{40}}\times{\color{blue}{3}} = 120$ miles

- after ${\color{blue}{4}}$ hours, the car covers a distance of ${\color{red}{40}}\times{\color{blue}{4}} = 160$ miles

- $\cdots$

This suggests the following formula:

$$
\text{distance} = \text{speed} \times \text{time}
$$

We can use this formula to calculate the distance traveled by an object moving at a constant speed.

For instance, suppose an elevator traveled for $1.5$ minutes at a constant speed of $120$ feet per minute. What distance is covered by the elevator?

The speed is $120$ feet per minute. To find the distance covered in $1.5$ minutes, we multiply the speed by $1.5.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{distance} & =\text{speed}\times \text{time} \\  & =120\times 1.5 \\  & =180.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the elevator covered a distance of $180$ feet.

occurrences.title: Proof of the Formula
occurrences.content:
We know that the area formula for a triangle is

$$
\mathcal{A} = \dfrac{b \cdot h}{2},
$$

where $b$ is a base and $h$ is the corresponding height.

But where does this formula come from?

To understand where the formula comes from, consider $\triangle{ABC}$ below.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/ca6f0f235d553fa3278d1726334102fc)

Let's draw a rectangle around $\triangle{ABC},$ as follows:

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/2ccb505e1fe94085d7ed416d4fcfedd6)

We have two pairs of right triangles with equal areas (each pair is indicated with arrows).

So, the area of $\triangle{ABC}$ is exactly half of the area of the rectangle. This gives

$$
\mathcal{A}_{ABC} = \dfrac{AB \cdot CH}{2}.
$$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
The **area of a triangle** can be computed using the formula

$$
\mathcal{A} = \dfrac{b \cdot h}{2},
$$

where $b$ is a *base* of the triangle and $h$ is the corresponding *height*.

To demonstrate, let's compute the area of the triangle with base 
$b = 4$
and the corresponding height is
$h = 8,$
as shown below.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/fc113e09eff8eb7443efb28ada750225)

The area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{b\cdot h}{2} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 8}{2} \\  & =\frac{32}{2} \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** At the end of the lesson, we'll demonstrate where the formula comes from. But first, let's get some practice using it.

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Suppose that Katie took her dog to the park, and they entered the park walking at a speed of ![](/tmp/newer-review/graphics/95836ae470c61ab15bfb67d6f0c92d2ad8d03d400b04473e81e58de3ee44bf32.svg) meter per second. However, the dog then saw a squirrel across the field and began sprinting toward it. After ![](/tmp/newer-review/graphics/0cf2eee0cdec31b7acdc244a255aaee7d6d520cfeee67b64ac9cf215f5377477.svg) seconds, the dog had reached a speed of ![](/tmp/newer-review/graphics/c700188055bde6c02303571bfb6b737fddda4a14c08edf1cdeeaf684530eea88.svg) meters per second.

We can represent this information visually using a **speed-time** graph, where speed is plotted as a function of time. To construct the speed-time graph, we use the given information to find two points on the graph.
