\begin{aligned}{[\operatorname{cos}(3\theta )+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}(3\theta )]}^{5} & =\operatorname{cos}(5\cdot 3\theta )+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}(5\cdot 3\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}(15\theta )+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}(15\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Consider the standard basis $\big\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \big\}$ of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the unit square spanned by these two vectors. 

Let's define a linear transformation $\mathbf R$ by its standard matrix $R,$ given by 

$$
[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘} & -\operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘} \\ \operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘} & \operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘}\end{aligned}]
$$

We can find the images of $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ under $\mathbf{R}$ by computing the matrix products, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{'} & =R(i)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘} & -\operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘} \\ \operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘} & \operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘} \\ \operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘}\end{aligned}] \\ {j}^{'} & =R(j)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘} & -\operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘} \\ \operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘} & \operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘} \\ \operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Plotting the vectors $\mathbf i$ and $\mathbf j$ and their images $\mathbf i'$ and $\mathbf j',$ we obtain the following:

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/b191cb068776f81a39fb9de5734cb043)

We see that the transformation $\mathbf R$ represented by the matrix $R$ defines a **counterclockwise rotation of $30^\circ$ about the origin.**

As usual, we typically refer to rotations in the counterclockwise sense. However, in this case, the transformation $\mathbf R$ can also be considered a rotation of $360^\circ-30^\circ=330^\circ$ *clockwise* about the origin.

occurrences.title: General Rotation Matrix
occurrences.content:
The matrix $R_\theta,$ given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}\theta  & -\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}\theta  & \operatorname{cos}\theta \end{aligned}]
$$

represents a **rotation by an angle $\theta$ counterclockwise about the origin.**

To find the matrix representing a rotation by an angle $\theta$ *clockwise* about the origin, we replace $\theta$ with $-\theta$ in the above. This gives

$$
[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}(-\theta ) & -\operatorname{sin}(-\theta ) \\ \operatorname{sin}(-\theta ) & \operatorname{cos}(-\theta )\end{aligned}]
$$

occurrences.title: Trapezoidal Rule Sum with Irregular Step Size
occurrences.content:
So far, the step size $\Delta x$ has been the same for each trapezoid. In these cases, we say that the step size is **regular**.

However, in some situations, the step size can vary. In such cases, we say that the step size is **irregular**. But we can still use the trapezoidal rule to approximate the area under a curve. Let's see an example.

occurrences.title: The General Formula
occurrences.content:
In the previous problem, we had the following expression for the trapezoidal rule sum:

$$
\mathcal{A} \approx \dfrac{ {\color{red}f(1)}+{\color{red}f(2)} }{2}\cdot {\color{blue}\Delta x} + \dfrac{ {\color{red}f(2)}+ {\color{red}f(3)} }{2}\cdot {\color{blue}\Delta x} + \dfrac{ {\color{red}f(3)}+ {\color{red}f(4)} }{2}\cdot {\color{blue}\Delta x}
$$

Notice that we can simplify the above by factoring out $\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $\Delta x,$ and also collecting like terms:

$$
\mathcal{A} \approx \dfrac{1}{2} [ \overbrace{{\color{red}f(1)} + 2\left( {\color{red}f(2)}+{\color{red}f(3)}\right) +{\color{red}f(4)}}^{\color{red}\large\text{bases}} ] \underbrace{\color{blue}\Delta x}_{\color{blue}\large\text{height}}
$$

In general, we can compute the trapezoidal rule sum for a function $y=f(x)$ over an interval $[a,b]$ using the **general formula** as follows:

$$
\mathcal{A} \approx \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot [\overbrace{{\color{red}f(a)} + 2({\color{red}f(x_1)}+{\color{red}f(x_2)}+ \ldots +{\color{red}f(x_{n-1})}) +{\color{red}f(b)} }^{\color{red}\large\text{bases}} ] \cdot\!\! \underbrace{\color{blue}\Delta x}_{\color{blue}\large\text{height}},
$$

Here, $n$ is the number of trapezoids, and $\Delta x$ is the step size given by

$$
\Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}.
$$

**Note:** If we look carefully at the formula, we realize that the trapezoidal rule is an average of the left and right Riemann sums!

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Suppose that we wish to approximate the area ![](/tmp/newer-review/graphics/6bd69882ede929379fa9babdf49386dd09138f26cabc6a4d617bbac5e92d21a5.svg) under the curve ![](/tmp/newer-review/graphics/2eb046be7e52e5a72d29a1333f9cf483411f0a8d6d897fe53014cc1952c6f759.svg) on the interval ![](/tmp/newer-review/graphics/ef1ae5c1ba5a449d816bfb51a4a5d469ea802406b197a04c15e1c885c5e295b8.svg)

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/f44327b2354d4b50353a64c5fd029b09)

We have already seen how to estimate the area using left and right Riemann sums, in which we approximate the area using rectangles.

However, we can get an even better estimate using trapezoids instead. The process of approximating the area under a curve using trapezoids is called the **trapezoidal rule.**

Here, we will approximate the area under the graph of ![](/tmp/newer-review/graphics/2eb046be7e52e5a72d29a1333f9cf483411f0a8d6d897fe53014cc1952c6f759.svg) with three trapezoids, each with a height equal to ![](/tmp/newer-review/graphics/daae2fd3251c4ba175906af980d1c33d4db057c616509ec6a146307d64417228.svg) Note that the trapezoids are turned on their side, so *their heights run horizontally*.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/c05175dfb98fe8f7aafebf84d74063af)

We compute the area of each trapezoid and add them all together:

![](/tmp/newer-review/graphics/093f580f625b22a2cf914a85c64b433e280e30071df9c934ddef49af5034e1da.svg)

Because the function is *concave up* over the interval ![](/tmp/newer-review/graphics/8559262277e3f52fd1eb8139fad407ed50f80873ec56c7349969a9a3ee6789e4.svg) the trapezoids reach above the function, and therefore our approximation is an *overestimate* of the actual area.

occurrences.title: Solving Trigonometric Equations Using the Sin-Cos-Tan Identity Under a Modified Domain
occurrences.content:
Let's find all the solutions to the equation

$$
-\pi <x\le \pi .
$$

Notice that this time, the domain is $-\pi <  x \leq \pi.$

First, we divide each term of the equation by $\cos x$ and use the identity $\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ to simplify. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}x-\operatorname{cos}x & =0 \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}x}{\operatorname{cos}x}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}x}{\operatorname{cos}x} & =0 \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}x}{\operatorname{cos}x}-\frac{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}x}} & =0 \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}x}{\operatorname{cos}x}-1 & =0 \\ \operatorname{tan}x-1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\tan x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\tan x = 1
$$

We can immediately calculate the principal value $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
x =  \arctan(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}
$$

Since $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is $x_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

To find the other solution in the given interval, we *subtract* $\pi.$ Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-\pi  \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}-\pi  \\  & =-\frac{3\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So the solutions are $x = -\dfrac{3\pi}{4} , \dfrac{\pi}{4} .$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Suppose we want to find all of the solutions to the equation

$$
0\le x<2\pi .
$$

To calculate a solution, we can reduce the equation to a more convenient form by dividing through by $\cos x,$ and then use the identity $\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ to simplify. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}x-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}x & =0 \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}x}{\operatorname{cos}x}-\frac{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}x}{\operatorname{cos}x} & =0 \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}x}{\operatorname{cos}x}-\frac{\sqrt{3}\cancel{\operatorname{cos}x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}x}} & =0 \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}x}{\operatorname{cos}x}-\sqrt{3} & =0 \\ \operatorname{tan}x-\sqrt{3} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\tan x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\tan x = \sqrt{3}
$$

We can immediately calculate the principal value $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
x = \arctan(\sqrt{3}) = \dfrac{\pi}{3}
$$

Since $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is $x_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{3}.$

To find the other solution in the given interval, we add $\pi\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}+\pi  \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}+\pi  \\  & =\frac{4\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So the solutions are $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{4\pi}{3}.$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
For a function $f(x),$ its derivative at a point $x$ is defined by the limit

$$
f'(x) = \lim\limits_{h\to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x) }{h}.
$$

But often, computing this limit exactly is impossible or impractical. One example might be when we don't have an explicit expression for $f(x).$ In such cases, instead of finding an exact value for $f'(x)$, we can *approximate* the derivative using the formula

 

$$
f'(x)\approx \frac{f(x+h) - f(x) }{h}
$$

for small values of the "step size" $h,$ with $h>0.$

This expression is called the **forward difference approximation** because if $h >0$ then $x+h$ is a step forward (i.e., to the right) from $x.$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/58c0fc28ed1e2bb0698d1789623d448e)

Generally, this and other similar methods are known as **finite-difference** approximations. The smaller the value of $h,$ the better the approximation.

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
To approximate the derivative of a function, we can use the finite difference formula

$$
f'(x)\approx \frac{f(x) - f(x-h) }{h}
$$

for small values of the step size $h,$ with $h>0.$

This expression is known as the **backward difference approximation** because if $h>0$ then $x-h$ is a step behind $x$ (i.e., to the left). 

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/47c63598a080abcea1b31b02005e5d6b)

As usual, the smaller the step size $h$ is, the better the approximation to $f'(x)$ we obtain.

occurrences.title: Derivation of the Formula
occurrences.content:
Where does the formula for the backward difference come from? Remember that from the definition of derivative, we have the forward difference formula

$$
f'(x)\approx \frac{f(x+h) - f(x) }{h}
$$

for small values of  $h.$ 

Now, replacing $h$ with $-h$ in the formula above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & \approx \frac{f(x-h)-f(x)}{-h} \\  & =\frac{f(x)-f(x-h)}{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

The step of replacing $h$ with $-h$ is equivalent to stepping a distance of $h$ to the left rather than to the right.

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
We've learned two methods for approximating the value of the derivative at a point by computing the rate of change between two points a distance of $h$ apart, where $h$ is small.

- The forward difference approximation computes the rate of change between the point $x$ and the point $x+h,$ which is a step of $h$ units forward.

$$
f'(x)  \approx \dfrac{f(x+h)- f(x)}{h}
$$

- The backward difference approximation computes the rate of change between the point $x$ and the point $x-h,$ which is a step of $h$ units backward.

$$
f'(x)  \approx \dfrac{f(x)- f(x-h)}{h}
$$

Now, we will introduce the **central difference approximation**, also known as the **symmetric difference approximation**. In this approximation, we compute the rate of change between the points $x-h$ and $x+h,$ a distance of $2h$ apart.

$$
f'(x)  \approx \dfrac{f(x+h)- f(x-h)}{2h}
$$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/be1a002b96b37dbf3658aaf471376e4c)

Usually, the central difference approximation is a better approximation for $f '(x)$ than the forward difference approximation and the backward difference approximation. This is because for the central difference approximation, $x$ is the midpoint between the two points $x-h$ and $x+h$ that are used in the approximation.

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Any curve defined using polar coordinates $(r(\theta), \theta)$ is a parametric curve in the parameter $\theta.$ For this reason, we can use the formula for differentiating parametric curves to compute the derivative of a polar curve:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}
$$

As an example, suppose we want to find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r = \sin4\theta,$ shown below.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/d6d940fd7c73fc6fbabc561f770e4f31)

First, recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x(\theta) = r \cos \theta, \qquad y(\theta) = r \sin \theta.
$$

Now, using the fact that $r=\sin 4\theta$ for this particular curve, we get

$$
x(\theta) = \sin 4\theta \cos\theta, \qquad y(\theta) =\sin4\theta \sin\theta.
$$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate $x'(\theta)$ and $y'(\theta)\mathbin{:}$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta$ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(\theta ) & =(\operatorname{sin}4\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta )^{'} \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}4\theta )^{'}\cdot \operatorname{cos}\theta +\operatorname{sin}4\theta \cdot (\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{'} \\  & =(4\operatorname{cos}4\theta )\cdot \operatorname{cos}\theta +\operatorname{sin}4\theta \cdot (-\operatorname{sin}\theta ) \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}4\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta -\operatorname{sin}4\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta$ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{'}(\theta ) & =(\operatorname{sin}4\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta )^{'} \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}4\theta )^{'}\cdot \operatorname{sin}\theta +\operatorname{sin}4\theta \cdot (\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{'} \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}4\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}\theta +\operatorname{sin}4\theta \cdot (\operatorname{cos}\theta ) \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}4\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta +\operatorname{sin}4\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{'}(\theta )}{{x}^{'}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{4\operatorname{cos}4\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta +\operatorname{sin}4\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta }{4\operatorname{cos}4\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta -\operatorname{sin}4\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

occurrences.title: Intuition Behind the Formula
occurrences.content:
We've been using the following formula for the area of the region bounded by a polar curve $r=r(\theta)$ and the rays $\theta=\theta_1$ and $\theta=\theta_2{:}$

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2 \:\textrm{d}\theta
$$

But where does this formula come from?

To see where the formula comes from, we can think about breaking up the area bounded by a polar curve into infinitesimally small sectors of circles.

As shown in the graph below, each sector has a radius of $r$ and spans an infinitesimally small angle, $\textrm d \theta.$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/f54818e0e1def6c498e34fd18ddf6925)

The ratio of the area of a sector to the full area of the circle must be the same as the ratio of the angle of the sector to a full revolution of the circle. So, if the area of a sector is $\textrm dA,$ then we can set up and solve the following proportion:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm dA}{\pi r^2} = \dfrac{\textrm d\theta}{2\pi} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \textrm dA = \dfrac{1}{2} r^2 \textrm d\theta
$$

Finally, to find the area under the curve, we can integrate the areas of all the sectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Suppose we want to find the area of the region bounded by the polar curve $r = 3\cos\theta$ and the rays $\theta_1 = 0$ and $\theta_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{2},$ as shown in blue in the picture below. Can we calculate this area using polar coordinates?

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/0ae57c37a8bcd46584a48b6258ff7d47)

In general, the area of the region bounded by a polar curve $r=r(\theta)$ and the rays $\theta=\theta_1$ and $\theta=\theta_2$ is given by the formula

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2 \:\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Therefore, the area of the half-circle above can be obtained as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(3\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{2}(1+\operatorname{cos}(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{4}(\theta {|}_{0}^{\pi /2}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}(2\theta ){|}_{0}^{\pi /2}) \\  & =\frac{9}{4}(\frac{\pi }{2}+0) \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{8}\end{aligned}
$$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Consider the following geometric sequence: 

$$
3,\quad 6,\quad 12,\quad 24, \quad \ldots
$$

 

Suppose we want to find the first term that exceeds $3\,000\,000.$ We can do this by creating and solving an inequality.

First, let's construct a formula for the $n$th term of the sequence. The first term of the sequence is $a_1=3,$ and the common ratio is

$$
r = \dfrac 6 3 = 2.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =3\cdot {2}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be greater than $3\,000\,000.$ So, we can set up and solve the corresponding inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & >3\,000\,000 \\ 3\cdot {2}^{n-1} & >3\,000\,000 \\ {2}^{n-1} & >1\,000\,000 \\ \operatorname{log}({2}^{n-1}) & >\operatorname{log}(1\,000\,000) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}(2) & >\operatorname{log}(1\,000\,000) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}(1\,000\,000)}{\operatorname{log}(2)} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}(1\,000\,000)}{\operatorname{log}(2)}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
\dfrac {\log (1\,000\,000)} {\log (2)} + 1 \approx 20.932.
$$

Therefore, the $21$st term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $3\,000\,000.$

To check our answer, we can easily verify that $a_{20} < 3\, 000\, 000$ and $a_{21} > 3\, 000\, 000\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{20} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{20-1}=3\cdot {2}^{19}=1\,572\,864<3\,000\,000 \\ {a}_{21} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{21-1}=3\cdot {2}^{20}=3\,145\,728>3\,000\,000\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, $a_{21}$ is indeed the first term that exceeds $3\,000\,000.$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Recall that the equation of a horizontal hyperbola centered at $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
\dfrac{(x-h)^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{(y-k)^2}{b^2} = 1.
$$

The equations of the asymptotes of this horizontal hyperbola, as depicted in the diagram below, are

$$
y - k = \pm \dfrac b a (x - h).
$$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/f79b577466f57b1f93a9e0608cd11da1)

On the other hand, the equation of a vertical hyperbola centered at $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
\dfrac{(y-k)^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{(x-h)^2}{b^2} = 1.
$$

The equations of the asymptotes of this vertical hyperbola are

$$
y - k = \pm \dfrac a b (x - h).
$$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/3bf30f827eca1dac0164aca7932a52aa)

**Note:** To remember which formula to use for the asymptotes of a hyperbola, notice that the numerator of the fraction is always the constant associated with $y$ in the equation:

$$
y - k = \pm \dfrac{\textrm{constant associated with }y}{\textrm{constant associated with }x} (x - h)
$$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Consider a marble moving in a horizontal plane along the curve $y=2x^2-x,$ as shown below.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/ec355d823fcf96b011e214ccad2f60da)

Let $x$ and $y$ be the coordinates of the marble's position at time $t.$ Since the $x$- and $y$-coordinates of the marble's position change with time, we can write

$$
x = x(t),\qquad y=y(t).
$$

Note that

- the velocity of the marble in the $x$-direction is $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t},$ and

- the velocity of the marble in the $y$-direction is $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}.$

These velocities are said to be **related rates** because if we know one, we can easily compute the other. 

For example, suppose we know that $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}=3$ when $x=2.$ Let's use this information to compute $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}$ at this point. 

To calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t},$ we start with the equation 

$$
y=2x^2-x.
$$

 

Then, we differentiate both sides with respect to $t.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{x}^{2}-x) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{x}^{2}-x).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, note the following:

- We cannot explicitly differentiate the right-hand side with respect to $t$ because it's written as a function of $x$ only.

- To get around this problem, we use implicit differentiation: We differentiate the right-hand side with respect to $x,$ and then multiply the result by $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}.$

By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{x}^{2}-x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2}-x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (4x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}=3, \qquad x=2,
$$

and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =3\cdot (4\cdot 2-1)=21.\end{aligned}
$$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
The binomial theorem can be used to find or approximate the value of a number raised to a positive integer power. 

For example, suppose we want to approximate the numerical value of $(1.01)^{15}.$ A good place to start is the special case of the binomial formula:

$$
(1+x)^n = 1 + nx + \dfrac{1}{2!} n(n-1)x^2 + \cdots + x^n
$$

Notice that substituting $x={\color{blue}{0.01}}$ and $n={\color{red}{15}}$ gives 

$$
(1 + {\color{blue}{0.01}})^{\color{red}{15}} = 1 + {\color{red}{15}}({\color{blue}{0.01}}) + \dfrac{1}{2!} {\color{red}{15}}({\color{red}{15}}-1)({\color{blue}{0.01}})^2 + \cdots + ({\color{blue}{0.01}})^{\color{red}{15}}
$$

which simplifies as

$$
(1.01)^{15} = 1 + 15(0.01) + \dfrac{1}{2!} 15(14)(0.01)^2 + \cdots + (0.01)^{15}. \qquad\left(\ast\right)
$$

So, we can find the exact value of $(1.01)^{15}$ by evaluating the right-hand side of $\left(\ast\right).$ However, the full binomial expansion on the right-hand side contains $16$ terms! In cases like this, a good alternative is to find an approximation. 

Increasing powers of $x$ become progressively smaller when $x$ is small. In our case, this means 

$$
(0.01) \quad\gg\quad (0.01)^2 \quad\gg\quad (0.01)^3 \quad\gg\quad\cdots \quad\gg \quad(0.01)^{15}
$$

where the symbol $\gg$ means "much greater than." Therefore, we can find a good approximation of $(1.01)^{15}$ by considering the first few terms of $(\ast)$ only. 

If we drop everything but the first three terms of $\left(\ast\right),$ we arrive at the approximation

$$
(1.01)^{15} \approx 1 + 15(0.01) + \dfrac{1}{2!} 15(14)(0.01)^2 .
$$

Evaluating the right-hand side of the above, we get

$$
(1.01)^{15} \approx 1+0.15+0.0105 = 1.1605.
$$

Note that the exact value is

$$
(1.01)^{15} = 1.160\,968\ldots
$$

so our approximation is pretty good. However, if we want to improve our approximation, we must keep more terms from the original expansion.

occurrences.title: Approximating Powers of Numbers Using the Binomial Theorem
occurrences.content:
Up to now, we've seen how to approximate numbers of the form $(1+x)^n,$ where $x$ is small. 

To approximate numbers of the form $(a+b)^n$ where $a$ is any number, and $b$ is small, we need to apply the more general binomial theorem:

$$
{(a + b)^n} = {n \choose 0}{a^n}{b^0} + {n \choose 1}{a^{n - 1}}{b^1} + {n \choose 2}{a^{n - 2}}{b^2} + \cdots + {n \choose n}{a^0}{b^n}
$$

Let's see an example.

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
In the figure below, the parametric curve $x=2t,y=t^2-3t$ and the line $x-y-4=0$ intersect at two points, $A$ and $B.$ How do we find the coordinates of these points?

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/252801494179bacee7632c1a590077f9)

To find the coordinates of the intersection points, we perform the following two steps.

**Step 1:** Take the equation of the line, replace $x$ and $y$ with the parametric formulas, and then solve for the parameter $t.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y-4 & =0 \\ (2t)-({t}^{2}-3t)-4 & =0 \\ 2t-{t}^{2}+3t-4 & =0 \\ -{t}^{2}+5t-4 & =0 \\ {t}^{2}-5t+4 & =0 \\ (t-1)(t-4) & =0 \\ t & =1,4.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2:** Find the coordinates of the intersection points by evaluating the parametric curve at these values of $t.$

- Let's start with $t=1.$ For $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2t \\ x & =2(1) \\ x & =2,\end{aligned}
$$

and for $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={t}^{2}-3t \\ y & =(1)^{2}-3(1) \\ y & =1-3 \\ y & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

So the coordinates of the first intersection point are $(2,-2).$

- Next, we consider $t=4.$ For $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2t \\ x & =2(4) \\ x & =8,\end{aligned}
$$

and for $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={t}^{2}-3t \\ y & =(4)^{2}-3(4) \\ y & =16-12 \\ y & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

So the coordinates of the second intersection point are $(8,4).$

Therefore, the curve $x=2t,y=t^2-3t$ intersects the line $x-y-4=0$ at the points $(2,-2)$ and $(8,4).$

occurrences.title: Vertical Stretch
occurrences.content:
Now, let $[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]$ be a matrix of a linear transformation $\mathbf T.$ We can find the images of $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ under $\mathbf T$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{'} & =T(i)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=i \\ {j}^{'} & =T(j)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=2j\end{aligned}
$$

Applying this transformation, we obtain the following image:

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/d4281f0df958135cfc892c1765a3df06)

The transformation represented by the matrix $T$ multiplies the vector $\mathbf{j}$ by $2$ and leaves the vector $\mathbf i$ unchanged. This type of transformation is called a **stretch in the $\mathbf y$-direction.** We can also call this a **vertical stretch**. In this case, we have a **vertical stretch of scale factor** $\mathbf 2$. 

In general, a stretch in the $y$-direction of scale factor $k$ with its center at the origin is represented by the matrix

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & k\end{aligned}]
$$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Consider the standard basis $\big\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \big\}$ of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the unit square spanned by the vectors.

Let $[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$ be a matrix of a linear transformation $\mathbf T.$ We can find the images of $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ under $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{'} & =T(i)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=2i \\ {j}^{'} & =T(j)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=j\end{aligned}
$$

Applying this transformation, we obtain the following image:

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/913f713af57050bff01b5e79203d8e02)

We see that the transformation represented by the matrix $T$ multiplies the vector $\mathbf{i}$ by a factor of $2$ and leaves the vector $\mathbf j$ unchanged. This type of transformation is called a **stretch in the $\mathbf x$-direction.** We can also call it a **horizontal stretch.** In this case, we have a **horizontal stretch of scale factor** $\mathbf 2.$

In general, a stretch in the $x$-direction of scale factor $k$ with its center at the origin is represented by the matrix

$$
[\begin{aligned}k & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

occurrences.title: Horizontal Shear
occurrences.content:
Consider the standard basis $\big\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \big\}$ of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the unit square spanned by the vectors.

Let $[\begin{aligned}1 & 0.5 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$ be a matrix of a linear transformation $\mathbf T.$ We can find the images of $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ under $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{'} & =T(i)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0.5 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=i \\ {j}^{'} & =T(j)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0.5 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=0.5i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Applying this transformation, we obtain the following image:

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/12b52dfba1b01fdd1f6a270330eef8d8)

The transformation represented by the matrix $T$ adds $0.5\mathbf{i}$ to $\mathbf j,$ while the vector $\mathbf i$ remains unchanged. This type of transformation is called a **horizontal shear.** In this case, we have a **horizontal shear with a shear factor of** $\mathbf{0.5}.$

In general, a horizontal shear of scale factor $k$ with its center at the origin is represented by the matrix

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & k \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

occurrences.title: Vertical Shear
occurrences.content:
Now, let $[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 1\end{aligned}]$ be a matrix of a linear transformation $\mathbf T.$ We can find the images of $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ under $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{'} & =T(i)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0.5\end{aligned}]=i+0.5j \\ {j}^{'} & =T(j)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=j\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the following image:

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/ca5278fc7c512c32157435f321b3e215)

The transformation represented by the matrix $T$ adds $0.5\mathbf{j}$ to $\mathbf i,$ while the vector $\mathbf j$ remains unchanged. This type of transformation is called a **vertical shear.** In this case, we have a **vertical shear with a shear factor of** $\mathbf{0.5}.$

In general, a vertical shear of scale factor $k$ with its center at the origin is represented by the matrix

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ k & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Suppose we are given two linear transformations represented by the matrices

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Here, $R$ represents a rotation of $90^\circ$ counterclockwise about the origin, and $S$ represents a reflection in the $x$-axis. Now, let $\mathbf{v}$ be a vector on the plane. Let's apply $R$ and then $S$ (in this particular order) to $\mathbf{v}.$ We obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}v\overset{R}{⟶}Rv\overset{S}{⟶}S(Rv)\end{aligned}
$$

The above states that $\mathbf{v}$ under the action of $R$ is mapped to $R\mathbf{v},$ and then $R\mathbf{v}$ under the action of $S$ is mapped to $S(R\mathbf{v}).$

Since matrix multiplication is associative, we can write

$$
S(R\mathbf{v}) = (SR)\mathbf{v}.
$$

So, the product $SR$ (in this particular order) represents the combined transformation. 

In our case, the matrix that represents the combined transformation is

$$
\begin{aligned}SR & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

occurrences.title: The Order in Which Transformations Are Applied
occurrences.content:
The order in which the multiplication is carried out is extremely important! 

For example, consider the transformations 

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Computing the product $SR,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}SR=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the transformation $SR$ represents a reflection in line $y=-x.$ 

On the other hand, computing the product $RS,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}RS=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The product $RS$ represents a reflection in line $y=x,$ which is a completely different transformation than $SR.$ 

In general, the transformations are performed from right-to-left. So, for example, if we have

$$
\mathbf v' = SR\mathbf v,
$$

then we should think of the transformation $R$ as being applied *first*, followed by $S.$

**Note:** The reason why transformations are performed right-to-left is that the rightmost transformation is the first transformation preceding the input. In our case, to compute $SR \mathbf v,$

- we first apply $R$ to $\mathbf v$ to get $R \mathbf v,$

- and then we apply $S$ to $R \mathbf v$ to get $SR \mathbf v.$

occurrences.title: Why Does the Function Have to Be Continuous?
occurrences.content:
Consider the function $f(x)$ given below.

$$
{\begin{aligned}-x+5, & 1\le x<3 \\ -x+4, & 3\le x<4\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Can we apply the intermediate value theorem to $f(x)$ on the interval $[1,4]?$

Remember, the intermediate value theorem assumes that the function is continuous. Here, the function $f(x)$ not continuous on $[1,4].$ So, we cannot apply the intermediate value theorem.

If we plot the function, we can get an idea of why the intermediate value theorem cannot be applied.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/5688944a294cb6565f1f5991e11bc07e)

The graph shows that, for example, the equation $f(x)=1.5$ has no solution on $[1,4]$ despite the fact that $1.5$ lies between $f(1)=4$ and $f(4)=0.$
So, the intermediate value theorem does not hold.

**Watch out!** The interval on which we apply the intermediate value theorem must *always* be closed. For example, we can't apply the theorem on an interval like $[1,3).$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
The **intermediate value theorem (IVT)** states that:

> *If $f(x)$ is continuous on $\color{blue}[a,b],$ and $k$ is a number between $\color{red}{f(a)}$ and $\color{red}{f(b)}$ inclusively, then there exists a number $c \in \color{blue}{[a,b]}$ such that $f(c)=k.$*

The intuition behind the IVT is that if a function is continuous between two inputs, then between those two inputs, we must be able to draw the function without picking up our pen off the page, so the function must cover all values between the two corresponding outputs.

The IVT is often used to prove that some equation has a solution. For example, if we want to prove that there is a solution to $f(x)=3,$ and we know that $f(x)$ is a continuous function with $f({\color{blue}{1}})={\color{red}{2}}$ and $f({\color{blue}{6}})={\color{red}{6}},$ then the IVT tells us that there exists some solution $c \in \color{blue}{[1,6]}$ such that $f(c)=3.$

We can gain further intuition by visualizing the situation. First, let's plot what $y=f(x)$ *might* look like.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/37cd1acc19a6c3f1ec28de339987035d)

For this particular $f(x)$ there is one solution to $f(x)=3$, which is $x\approx 2.$ Note that our solution lies inside the interval $\color{blue}[1,6].$

Now let's consider another *possible* $f(x).$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/57f39e1bfa7c0834cbbcead1d0b6626b)

This time, there are three solutions to $f(x)=3$ which lie in the interval $\color{blue}[1,6].$ 

We can keep changing our $f(x),$ but no matter how we draw it, we will always have some solution to $f(x)=3$ which lies in the interval $\color{blue}[1,6].$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/a71554c73083dc0559d0f1ee69158ad3)

occurrences.title: Another Definition of the Exponential Function
occurrences.content:
Let's now consider the limit

$$
\lim_{n \to  \infty} \left(1+\dfrac{x}{n}\right)^{n},
$$

where $x$ is a real number.

First, we rewrite the given limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{x}{n})}^{n} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n/x})}^{n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n/x})}^{(n/x)\cdot x} \\  & ={[{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n/x})}^{n/x}]}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, since [math]n/x \to \infty[/math] as [math]n \to \infty,[/math] we have 

\[
\left[ \lim_{n \to \infty} \left(1+\dfrac{1}{\color{blue}n/x}\right)^{{\color{blue}n/x}} \right]^x = \left[ \lim_{{\color{blue}n/x} \to \infty} \left(1+\dfrac{1}{\color{blue}n/x}\right)^{{\color{blue}n/x}} \right]^x
\]

Let's now perform the substitution $m=n/x.$ Since $m\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{[{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n/x})}^{n/x}]}^{x} & =[\,{{{lim}_{m\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{m})}^{m}}_{⏟}}_{e}\,]^{x} \\  & ={e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{x}{n})}^{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Let's consider the following limit:

$$
\lim_{n \to  \infty} \left(1+\dfrac{1}{n}\right)^{n}
$$

Notice that as $n \to \infty,$ 

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1,$ while

- the exponent approaches $\infty.$

If we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
\lim_{n \to  \infty} \left(1+\dfrac{1}{n}\right)^{n} = 1^\infty,
$$

which is an indeterminate form (i.e., its meaning is ambiguous and therefore cannot be used to determine the true value of the limit). So, if we want to evaluate this limit, we need to find another way to do it.

To get a feel for how this limit behaves, we create a table of values, as follows:

| $n$ | $\left(1+\dfrac{1}{n}\right)^{n}$ |
| --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2.000\,00$ |
| $10$ | $2.593\,74$ |
| $100$ | $2.704\,81$ |
| $1\,000$ | $2.716\,92$ |
| $10\,000$ | $2.718\,15$ |
| $100\,000$ | $2.718\,27$ |
| $1\,000\,000$ | $2.718\,28$ |

Now, recall Euler's number $e\approx 2.718\,28$ to five decimal places. It appears that our expression converges to $e$ as $n\to\infty.$ It can be shown that this is indeed the case. 

Therefore, we have the following important result:

$$
e = \lim_{n \to  \infty} \left(1+\dfrac{1}{n}\right)^{n}
$$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
The parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation

$$
\dfrac{y^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{x^2}{b^2} = 1
$$

are given by 

$$
x=b\tan{t},\quad y=a\sec{t},
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. The domain of the parameter $t$ is

$$
t\in[-\pi,\pi],\qquad t\neq \pm \frac{\pi}{2}.
$$

The branches corresponding to different values of $t$ are shown in the diagram below.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/af5df25094578ebacde5afd40c5acff1)

This parametrization contains discontinuities at $t=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$ One consequence of this is that the curve appears to "jump" between different quadrants at the singular points.

For the most part, we won't worry too much about the domain of $t.$ However, it does become important when we're parametrizing part of a hyperbola, which we'll deal with later.

**Note:** To understand where this parametrization comes from, recall the trigonometric identity

$$
1 + \tan^2 t = \sec^2 t.
$$

Rearranging, we get

$$
\sec^2 t - \tan^2 t  =1,
$$

which means

$$
\begin{aligned}{sec}^{2}t & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}\,\Rightarrow \,y=a\operatorname{sec}t \\ {tan}^{2}t & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}\,\Rightarrow \,x=b\operatorname{tan}t.\end{aligned}
$$

occurrences.title: Proof That the Parametric Equations Describe a Vertical Hyperbola
occurrences.content:
We've used the fact that the parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin are

$$
x=b\tan{t},\quad y=a\sec{t}.
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants. Now, we'll demonstrate why this is true.

First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =b\operatorname{tan}t & ⟹ &  & \operatorname{tan}t & =\frac{x}{b}, \\ y & =a\operatorname{sec}t & ⟹ &  & \operatorname{sec}t & =\frac{y}{a}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall the secant-tangent identity:

$$
\tan^2{t} + 1 = \sec^2{t}.
$$

Substituting the above into the secant-tangent identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}t+1 & ={sec}^{2}t \\ {(\frac{x}{b})}^{2}+1 & ={(\frac{y}{a})}^{2} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}+1 & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{a}^{2}} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is the Cartesian equation of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin. Therefore, the parametric equations do indeed describe a vertical hyperbola.

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Consider the circle below. How do we calculate $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x},$ the slope of the tangent to this circle at any point on the circle? 

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/9e371d98c98186c022ba3c0ecc7ae5b9)

To calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}$, we start by writing down the equation of the circle. Then, we differentiate the equation of the circle with respect to $x.$

Since our circle is centered at the origin and has a radius of $\sqrt{5},$ its equation is given by

$$
x^2 + y^2 = (\sqrt{5})^2 
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x^2 + y^2 = 5.
$$

Now, to calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x},$ we differentiate the equation of the circle using implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 2x+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find the slope at any point on the circle using our expression for the derivative. 

For example, since the point $P\big( \sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3} \big)$ satisfies the equation $x^2 + y^2 = 5,$ it must lie on the circle. Therefore, the slope of the tangent at this point is given by

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} \Bigg|_{( \sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3})} = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} = -\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{3}.
$$

occurrences.title: Introduction
occurrences.content:
Suppose we are given the parabola 

$$
x^2 - 4x - 8y - 28 = 0,
$$

whose graph is shown below. How can we find the vertex of the parabola?

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/a37e99d5033ba8818d790b66baceff3e)

Recall that the standard equation of a *vertical* parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ is

$$
(x-h)^2 = 4p(y-k),
$$

where $p$ is a constant. 

To write our equation in standard form, we group the $x$-terms on the left-hand side and complete the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4x-8y-28 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-4x & =8y+28 \\ (x-2)^{2}-4 & =8y+28 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =8y+32 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =8(y+4) \\ (x-2)^{2} & =4(2)(y-(-4))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the vertex are $(h,k) = ({\color{blue}2},{\color{red}-4}).$
